prasangs.lesson: When duties collide, weigh them honestly, and keep your word to those who trust you.
prasangs.story_hook: A king put himself on the scale to save a bird that had come to him for help.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Vana CXXXI. Self-mutilation is graphic; retellings should stay gentle.

prasangs.title_en: Nahusha the python and Yudhishthira's answers
prasangs.summary: A giant python seizes Bhima. It is King Nahusha, once lord of heaven, cursed for making sages carry his palanquin. He frees Bhima after Yudhishthira answers his questions on goodness, and is freed himself.
prasangs.lesson: Success can blind anyone. What makes a person good is conduct, not birth.
prasangs.story_hook: The strongest Pandava lay crushed in the coils of a python that spoke like a king.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Vana CLXXVIII-CLXXXI (180 checked). The varna argument (3.182.20-37) is left out of cards.

prasangs.title_en: Draupadi and Satyabhama on marriage
prasangs.summary: Krishna's wife Satyabhama asks Draupadi what charm keeps her five husbands devoted. Draupadi says charms and manipulation destroy trust, then describes her own exhaustive care of the household.
prasangs.lesson: Love can't be managed or manipulated into place; trust grows only where no one feels controlled.
prasangs.notes: CAUTION: most of the chapter prescribes one-sided wifely service and husbands as gods (3.234.20-41, 3.235). Use only the anti-manipulation point; avoid as a story day without careful framing.

prasangs.title_en: Savitri and Satyavan
prasangs.summary: Princess Savitri marries Satyavan knowing he will die within a year. On the fated day she follows Yama, the lord of death, speaking such wisdom about goodness and friendship that he grants boon after boon, until she wins back her husband's life.
prasangs.lesson: Steady love and clear speech can face even death. Determination carries what fear would drop.
prasangs.story_hook: Savitri knew the exact day her husband would die, and she went into the forest with him anyway.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Vana CCXCII-CCXCVI (294, 295 checked). The 'pativrata' framing is the text's; retell it as courage and love.

prasangs.title_en: Nala and Damayanti
prasangs.summary: King Nala, possessed by the spirit Kali, gambles away his kingdom to his brother and abandons Damayanti in the forest. Years of separation and disguise follow, until Nala masters the dice and the two are reunited.
prasangs.lesson: Compulsions can take everything. Loyalty and patience can still bring you home.
prasangs.story_hook: The more King Nala lost at dice, the less he could stop.
prasangs.notes: Told to Yudhishthira, himself ruined by dice. Few lines stand alone; Nala's abandonment of his sleeping wife needs honest handling in a retelling.

prasangs.title_en: Vyadha Gita: the butcher who taught a sage
prasangs.summary: A proud ascetic, Kaushika, is sent to learn from a meat-seller in Mithila. The butcher teaches him plain goodness: don't return evil, repent and resolve, keep envy away, care for your parents, and don't spend your one life making enemies.
prasangs.lesson: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.
prasangs.notes: Narrated by Markandeya in the Markandeya-samasya. Data 3.210 = Ganguli CCVI. The butcher's caste/trade defence (3.212) excluded.

prasangs.title_en: Yaksha Prashna: the questions at the lake
prasangs.summary: One by one, four Pandavas drink from a lake against a voice's warning and fall dead. Yudhishthira answers the Yaksha's riddles instead, and when offered one brother's life, chooses his stepmother's son Nakula, out of fairness.
prasangs.lesson: Answer life's questions with a steady mind, and let kindness outweigh advantage.
prasangs.story_hook: Four brothers lay dead by a clear lake, and the voice that killed them was asking Yudhishthira riddles.
prasangs.notes: Q&A is 3.314.47-124; data runs about three ahead of Ganguli CCCXI-CCCXIII.

prasangs.title_en: After the war: Yudhishthira's grief and his family's counsel
prasangs.summary: Victorious but shattered by the deaths of kin, Yudhishthira wants to give up the throne for the forest. Arjuna, Bhima, Draupadi, Nakula, the sage Devasthana and Vyasa each argue with him, about duty, guilt, grief and the shortness of life, until he agrees to rule.
prasangs.lesson: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.
prasangs.story_hook: He had won the war, and all Yudhishthira wanted was to walk into the forest and never come back.
prasangs.notes: Range approximate (12.7-12.36). Arjuna's speech on wealth (12.8) is cynical and not carded.

prasangs.title_en: Ashma Gita: the sage on bearing loss
prasangs.summary: Vyasa tells the grieving Yudhishthira how the sage Ashma consoled King Janaka: pain comes from what we didn't want or what we lost; meetings end; days don't return; ask who you are and steady the mind.
prasangs.lesson: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Santi XXVIII (inferred). Its run of fate verses (27.16-32) is excluded.

prasangs.title_en: The sixteen kings: Narada consoles Srinjaya
prasangs.summary: Krishna tells Yudhishthira how Narada consoled King Srinjaya, whose son had died, by recounting sixteen legendary kings far greater than his son who also died. Moved, Srinjaya listens, and Narada restores the boy.
prasangs.lesson: Everyone we love is mortal; you are not singled out. Grief can still be met with care.
prasangs.story_hook: A king could not stop weeping for his son, so a sage began telling him about everyone else who had died.
prasangs.notes: Chapter 12.28 is long catalogue; best as a retold story, not cards.

prasangs.title_en: Bhishma on friends and kinsmen
prasangs.summary: Bhishma explains the kinds of friends, how to recognise the best friend, and the double nature of relatives: they can be rivals, yet when outsiders wrong you, family is your refuge.
prasangs.lesson: A true friend isn't stung by your success. Family is difficult, and still your refuge.
prasangs.notes: Rajadharma; some lines are cynical about trust (80.9-14) and are not carded.

prasangs.title_en: Krishna's family troubles: the weapon not made of iron
prasangs.summary: Even Krishna struggles with his clan: he does their work, bears their harsh words, and feels like the mother of two gamblers playing each other. Narada tells him the only weapon that works is soft: generosity, patience, sincerity, gentleness and respect.
prasangs.lesson: In family feuds, the weapon that works is gentleness, patience and respect.
prasangs.story_hook: Krishna, who guided a war, admitted to a sage that he could not keep the peace in his own family.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Santi LXXXI (checked).

prasangs.title_en: Brihaspati on winning people with speech
prasangs.summary: Indra asks Brihaspati what single thing wins people over. Gentle, welcoming speech, says Brihaspati: speak first, with a smile; a gift without kind words pleases no one.
prasangs.lesson: Kind words, spoken first and with warmth, win more than gifts.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Santi LXXXIV.

prasangs.title_en: Bhishma on mother, father and teacher
prasangs.summary: Asked which duty matters most, Bhishma names honouring one's mother, father and teachers, ranks the mother above all, and the teacher who gives knowledge highest of all.
prasangs.lesson: Honour the people who raised and taught you; a mother's worth is beyond measure.
prasangs.notes: 108.4-5 (obey them even against dharma) and 108.30-31 (sin of neglect) excluded as obedience/shame lines.

prasangs.title_en: Kalakavrikshiya consoles the fallen prince
prasangs.summary: Prince Kshemadarshi has lost his kingdom and wealth. The sage Kalakavrikshiya tells him grief has no power to restore what is gone, to want what is within reach, and to make peace with others' good fortune.
prasangs.lesson: Grief can't restore what's gone. Want what's within reach, and let others' success be.
prasangs.notes: Continues in 12.105 with a plan to ruin a rival kingdom, excluded.

prasangs.title_en: The river and the reeds
prasangs.summary: The Ocean asks the rivers why they uproot great trees but never the reeds. Ganga answers: the reed bends when the flood comes and stands again after; the rigid tree breaks.
prasangs.lesson: Bend with the flood and you stand again after it passes.
prasangs.story_hook: The rivers tore down mighty trees every monsoon, yet never the humble reeds on their banks.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Santi CXIII. Bending is adapting, not submitting to abuse.

prasangs.title_en: Bhishma on bearing slander
prasangs.summary: Yudhishthira asks how to respond when a harsh fool abuses you in public. Bhishma: let it pass like a crow cawing; the slanderer only displays his own faults.
prasangs.lesson: Careless critics show their own faults. Let their words pass like a crow's cawing.

prasangs.title_en: The cat and the mouse
prasangs.summary: Caught between a mongoose, an owl and a trapped cat, the mouse Palita makes a deal: he will gnaw the cat free if the cat protects him. Both keep the bargain, then part warily.
prasangs.lesson: Sometimes you must cooperate with a rival; do it with clear eyes.
prasangs.story_hook: A mouse, surrounded by enemies, decided the safest place was beside the cat.
prasangs.notes: Apaddharma; much of it is cynical ('no one is anyone's friend'). 12.138.3-5 contain '---' gaps.

prasangs.title_en: Bharadvaja's counsel on gentleness and firmness
prasangs.summary: A king asks how to deal with rivals. Most of the answer is hard-edged statecraft, but one line holds: gentleness wins over both the gentle and the harsh.
prasangs.lesson: Gentleness is sharper than harshness.
prasangs.notes: Largely realpolitik; one card only.

prasangs.title_en: The pigeons and the fowler
prasangs.summary: A storm-soaked fowler shelters under a tree after trapping a female pigeon. Her mate, grieving, still honours the fowler as a guest, lights a fire for him and, having nothing else, offers himself as food. The shaken fowler gives up hunting.
prasangs.lesson: Kindness can shame cruelty. Wherever the one you love is, that is home.
prasangs.story_hook: The hunter who had caught his wife was shivering under his tree, and the pigeon brought him fire.
prasangs.notes: Apaddharma. The pigeon's self-sacrifice should be retold as hospitality and the fowler's change of heart, not as a model.

prasangs.title_en: Gautama the ungrateful
prasangs.summary: A destitute brahmin, Gautama, is fed and sheltered by a kind crane, Rajadharma, and made rich by the crane's friend. On the way home he kills his sleeping benefactor for food. Bhishma ends: there is atonement for many wrongs, none for ingratitude.
prasangs.lesson: Gratitude is the root of every friendship. Betraying a benefactor poisons everything after.
prasangs.story_hook: The crane gave Gautama food, shelter and a fortune, and Gautama repaid him while he slept.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Santi CLXVIII-CLXXIII. Caste slurs in the story (12.172.13) are not used.

prasangs.title_en: King Senajit and the brahmin's consolation
prasangs.summary: King Senajit is crushed by his son's death. A brahmin comforts him: everyone suffers, no sorrow lasts forever, effort beats idleness, and whatever we call 'mine' becomes a source of pain.
prasangs.lesson: No one suffers forever. Meet what comes with an undefeated heart.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Santi CLXXIV. 'Do not form affection for children and kin' (173.17) excluded.

prasangs.title_en: Pingala's song: the night she stopped waiting
prasangs.summary: Pingala waited all night for a lover who never came. At last she saw that her peace depended on someone else's arrival, let the expectation go, and slept peacefully.
prasangs.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.
prasangs.story_hook: Pingala sat awake listening for footsteps that never came, until she stopped listening.
prasangs.notes: Pingala is a courtesan; tell it plainly and respectfully.

prasangs.title_en: Medhavin: the son who woke his father
prasangs.summary: A father lays out the conventional path of study, family and ritual. His son Medhavin replies that days and nights fall like arrows and death takes people mid-task, so do tomorrow's work today and live truthfully now.
prasangs.lesson: Life slips away while we stay busy. Do what matters now.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Santi CLXXV (checked). 174.38 ('what are wife and kin to you?') excluded.

prasangs.title_en: Shampaka on having little
prasangs.summary: A brahmin named Shampaka, in rags and poor, tells Bhishma why he weighed having nothing against a kingdom: the rich are always anxious, and without letting go no one sleeps without fear.
prasangs.lesson: Holding tight breeds anxiety. Letting go is what lets you sleep.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Santi CLXXVI. Not a case against earning; misuse note on 175.11.

prasangs.title_en: Manki's song: desire, I know your root
prasangs.summary: Manki spends all he has on a pair of oxen; both are killed in an accident. In his despair he sees through desire: it is born of his own imagining, and he resolves to forgive insults and stop feeding it. Bhishma adds Janaka's verse on owning nothing.
prasangs.lesson: Desire grows from what we imagine. Stop feeding it, and it fades.
prasangs.story_hook: Manki put every coin he had into two young oxen, and lost both in a single afternoon.
prasangs.notes: Data 12.176 merges Ganguli CLXXVII-CLXXVIII; Manki's fatalist line (176.12) excluded.

prasangs.title_en: Bodhya's teachers
prasangs.summary: Asked how he found peace, the sage Bodhya names his teachers: Pingala, the osprey that dropped its scrap of meat and was left alone, the snake, the deer, the arrow-maker so absorbed he did not see the king pass, and a girl's bangle.
prasangs.lesson: Learn from everything. Drop what makes you a target, and give your work full attention.
prasangs.notes: Data typo in 176.67 'इपावासक्त'.

prasangs.title_en: The python-sage (Ajagara vrata)
prasangs.summary: Prahlada meets a sage who lives like a python, taking what comes and not chasing. The sage explains how ceasing to chase made him content.
prasangs.lesson: Take what comes gladly; stop chasing what's out of reach.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Santi CLXXIX. The radical passivity is the sage's vow; cards take only the anti-chasing line.

prasangs.title_en: Kashyapa and the jackal: the gift of hands
prasangs.summary: A young brahmin, Kashyapa, knocked down by a rich man's chariot, wants to die in humiliation. A jackal tells him how lucky he is to have hands and a human life, and that craving grows like fire fed with wood. The jackal is Indra.
prasangs.lesson: You already have what others long for. Craving is a fire that more fuel only feeds.
prasangs.story_hook: Lying in the dust where a rich man's chariot had thrown him, Kashyapa wanted to die, and a jackal laughed at him.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Santi CLXXX. Kashyapa's wish to die is wounded pride, not depression; retell with care.

prasangs.title_en: Bali and Indra: the fortune that moves on
prasangs.summary: Indra, now king of the gods, finds his defeated rival Bali living as a donkey in an empty house and mocks him. Bali calmly answers that fortune has lived with a thousand Indras before, that time gives and takes, and that this is a season for calm.
prasangs.lesson: Success is on loan. Don't gloat in a good season or despair in a bad one.
prasangs.story_hook: The king of the gods went looking for his old enemy and found him living as a donkey.
prasangs.notes: Data 12.230-231 = Ganguli CCXXIII-CCXXIV (224 checked). Many verses are strongly fatalist; cards avoid them. 231.6 is garbled ('-------').

prasangs.title_en: Tuladhara and Jajali: the merchant who taught the ascetic
prasangs.summary: The ascetic Jajali, proud because birds nest in his matted hair, is told to learn from a trader in Varanasi. Tuladhara teaches that right living is being a friend to all in thought, word and deed, and dealing fairly.
prasangs.lesson: Goodness is everyday fairness and friendliness, not spiritual display.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Santi CCLXI-CCLXIV. Ahimsa arguments about sacrifice are not carded.

prasangs.title_en: Chirakari, the one who acts slowly
prasangs.summary: In a jealous rage, the sage Gautama orders his son Chirakari to kill his mother and storms off. Chirakari, famous for slowness, weighs a father's word against a mother's worth for so long that Gautama returns, regretful, and finds them both alive.
prasangs.lesson: In anger, and when loved ones seem to have wronged you, slow down.
prasangs.story_hook: Ordered by his furious father to kill his mother, Chirakari did what he always did: he thought about it.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Santi CCLXVI (checked). Contains violent premise; retellings should centre the slowness and the reconciliation.

prasangs.title_en: Hamsa Gita: the swan's teaching on speech and anger
prasangs.summary: Prajapati, in the form of a golden swan, answers the Sadhyas: never speak words that make others flinch, don't insult back, ride out the urges of speech and anger, and remember that we become our company.
prasangs.lesson: Words fly like arrows. The one who doesn't answer anger with anger stands highest.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Santi CCC (prior pass). Overlaps Vidura Niti 36 (Atreya); pick one per plan.

prasangs.title_en: Narada consoles Shuka
prasangs.summary: The sage Narada visits the young Shuka and teaches him how to meet sorrow: brooding doubles pain, the mind is healed by understanding as the body by medicine, act if you can fix it, and contentment is the real wealth.
prasangs.lesson: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Santi CCCXXX-CCCXXXI.

prasangs.title_en: Fate or effort? Brahma's answer
prasangs.summary: Yudhishthira asks which is stronger, destiny or human effort. Bhishma quotes Brahma: destiny is the seed, effort the field; without the field, the seed bears nothing.
prasangs.lesson: Luck is the seed, effort the field. Nothing grows without the field.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Anusasana VI.

prasangs.title_en: Bhishma on what ages and what doesn't
prasangs.summary: Bhishma explains how deeds follow their doer, and observes that hair, teeth, eyes and ears grow old while craving alone stays young.
prasangs.lesson: Everything in us ages except wanting. Notice it.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Anusasana VII (inferred).

prasangs.title_en: The parrot who stayed with the withered tree
prasangs.summary: A hunter's poisoned arrow withers the tree where a parrot has always lived. The parrot refuses to leave it. Indra, moved by its loyalty, restores the tree.
prasangs.lesson: Loyalty means staying through the bad season, not only the good.
prasangs.story_hook: Every other bird left the dying tree; the parrot stayed.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Anusasana V.

prasangs.title_en: Bhishma on everyday conduct
prasangs.summary: Asked what makes a life long and good, Bhishma answers: conduct. Be slow to anger and honest, greet your parents each morning, never mock anyone, and remember that a cruel word lodges in the heart.
prasangs.lesson: A good life is built from daily conduct: kind words, respect for elders, no mockery.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Anusasana CIV (checked). Much of the chapter is ritual purity, food and astrology rules, excluded.

prasangs.title_en: Bhishma on elder and younger siblings
prasangs.summary: Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should treat the younger ones. Bhishma: overlook small faults and correct gently, beware outsiders who sow division, divide property equally, and honour the mother above all.
prasangs.lesson: Overlook small faults, correct gently, share fairly, and don't let outsiders divide you.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Anusasana CV (checked). Framed around brothers and sons; cards widen to siblings and children.

prasangs.title_en: Brihaspati's golden rule
prasangs.summary: Brihaspati sums up all of right conduct in one line: don't do to others what would hurt you.
prasangs.lesson: Don't do to others what would hurt you.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Anusasana CXIII.

prasangs.title_en: Krishna on the war within
prasangs.summary: As Yudhishthira still grieves, Krishna tells him his real battle has begun: one fought alone, with his own mind, where 'mine' is death and 'not mine' is freedom.
prasangs.lesson: The hardest battle is with your own mind, and no one else can fight it for you.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Asvamedha XII-XIII.

prasangs.title_en: Kama Gita: the song of Desire
prasangs.summary: Krishna quotes Desire's own boast: whoever fights me with weapons, rituals, scripture, austerity or even the wish for liberation finds me reborn in that very method.
prasangs.lesson: A craving fought only with force comes back in a new form. Redirect it instead.
prasangs.notes: Krishna's answer (14.13.19) is to channel desire into dharma.

prasangs.title_en: Ambarisha's song: the kingdom within
prasangs.summary: King Ambarisha realises that the enemy he must conquer is his own greed, and sings that mastering it is the only kingdom worth having.
prasangs.lesson: Master your own greed. That is the only kingdom worth ruling.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Asvamedha XXXI. 14.32.1 is numeric placeholders in our data, so the range starts at 14.32.2.

prasangs.title_en: Uttanka confronts Krishna
prasangs.summary: Returning home after the war, Krishna meets the sage Uttanka, who is furious that Krishna let the cousins destroy each other and threatens to curse him. Krishna explains that he tried hard for peace and was refused, and calms him.
prasangs.lesson: You can try your best for peace and still fail. Others' choices are not your guilt.
prasangs.story_hook: The sage wanted to curse Krishna for the war, and Krishna asked him only to listen first.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Asvamedha LIII-LVIII. The later quest for the queen's earrings (14.56-58) is a separate adventure.

prasangs.title_en: The golden mongoose and the handful of flour
characters: The gleaner brahmin and his family
prasangs.summary: At the end of Yudhishthira's lavish horse sacrifice, a half-golden mongoose declares it worth less than a poor family's gift. In a famine, a gleaner, his wife, son and daughter-in-law each gave their last handful of flour to a hungry guest; rolling in the spilt flour turned half the mongoose to gold.
prasangs.lesson: A small gift, honestly earned and given from little, outweighs the grandest show.
prasangs.story_hook: Half of the mongoose was gold, and it had come to see if the emperor's sacrifice could gild the other half.
prasangs.notes: Ganguli Asvamedha XC (checked). The family going hungry should be told as generosity, not as a model of self-starvation.

prasangs.title_en: Grief becomes the first verse
prasangs.summary: Valmiki sees a hunter shoot one of a pair of mating cranes and hears the survivor cry. His grief bursts out as a curse that falls into rhythm; he regrets the words but realises they are a new kind of verse. Brahma tells him to use it to tell Ram's story.
prasangs.lesson: Grief can be turned into something that helps others; even a sage regrets words spoken in pain.
prasangs.story_hook: On the bank of the Tamasa, a poet watched a bird fall, and the sound that came out of him changed literature.

prasangs.title_en: Dasharatha lets his son go
prasangs.summary: The sage Vishvamitra asks the king for his teenage son Ram to protect a ritual. Dasharatha, who waited years for a child, refuses and offers himself and his army instead. His guru reminds him of his word and that the sage asks for Ram's own growth, and the king lets him go.
prasangs.lesson: Letting a child go out into the world can be the most loving thing a parent does.
prasangs.story_hook: The old king had waited sixty thousand years for a son, and now a stranger wanted to take him away.
prasangs.notes: Start is the last verse of sarga 18 (Vishvamitra's arrival).

prasangs.title_en: Bhagiratha brings the Ganga down
prasangs.summary: King Sagara's sixty thousand sons are burnt to ash; only the Ganga's water can free them. Sagara, his grandson Anshuman and Anshuman's son Dilipa each try and die without success. Bhagiratha finally persists until the river descends, and Brahma honours him for finishing what three generations began.
prasangs.lesson: Some goals take longer than one effort or one lifetime; keep going and others' work is not wasted.
prasangs.story_hook: Three kings in a row died trying to bring a river down from heaven; the fourth would not stop.
prasangs.notes: Mythic frame (ancestors' release) left in the background; the card value is generational persistence.

prasangs.title_en: The king who wanted the cow
prasangs.summary: King Vishvamitra is feasted by the sage Vasishtha and covets the wish-granting cow that made it possible. Vasishtha refuses every offer; the king takes her by force and is routed, then fails again with divine weapons. Humbled, he resolves to transform himself through inner discipline instead of force.
prasangs.lesson: Envy and force cannot take what someone will not give; real power is built inside.
prasangs.story_hook: A king who had everything saw one thing he could not buy, and it undid him.
prasangs.notes: Avoid the brahmin-versus-kshatriya framing of 1.56.16–1.56.17; tell it as envy, failure and a turn inward.

prasangs.title_en: Ten years gone: Vishvamitra and Menaka
prasangs.summary: Deep into his effort to transform himself, Vishvamitra falls for the nymph Menaka and ten years pass like a day. When he wakes up to it, he is ashamed, lets her go kindly rather than blaming her, and starts again. Brahma tells him he is not there yet: he must first master his senses.
prasangs.lesson: Lost years are not the end; notice, stop blaming, and begin again.
prasangs.story_hook: He looked up one morning and realised ten years had gone by.
prasangs.notes: Narrated by Shatananda to Ram. The sending of Menaka by Indra is a plot device; keep focus on the sage's recovery.

prasangs.title_en: Vishvamitra loses his temper, and begins again
prasangs.summary: Tested again, Vishvamitra explodes and curses the nymph Rambha, losing the fruit of his long effort. He vows not to give way to anger or speak in it, keeps a thousand-year silence, and this time obstacles shake him but anger cannot get in. He reaches his goal, and his old rival Vasishtha embraces him as a friend.
prasangs.lesson: Relapses happen; a clear vow and steady practice can make anger lose its grip, and rivals can become friends.
prasangs.story_hook: He had already started over once; then his temper threw it all away again.

prasangs.title_en: Ram and Sita's early marriage
prasangs.summary: Back in Ayodhya after the wedding, Ram and Sita settle into married life. Valmiki notes that their love, though it began as an arranged match, deepened because each came to know and value the other; she could read his heart without words.
prasangs.lesson: Love deepens by paying attention to who the other person really is.
prasangs.story_hook: Their marriage began as their fathers' arrangement; what happened next was their own.

prasangs.title_en: What Ram was like
prasangs.summary: Before the crisis, Valmiki and the citizens describe the young prince: gentle in speech, unprovoked by harshness, pleased by one kindness and forgetful of a hundred wrongs, humble about his strength, attentive to ordinary people's lives.
prasangs.lesson: Character shows in small habits: speaking first and gently, remembering kindness, forgetting slights.

prasangs.title_en: Kaikeyi's boons and the king's blind promise
prasangs.summary: The maid Manthara works on Queen Kaikeyi's insecurity until she is consumed by fear for her son's future. Kaikeyi makes the doting old king promise before she names her wish, then demands Ram's exile and Bharata's coronation. Bound by his word, Dasharatha pleads, rages and collapses.
prasangs.lesson: Envy grows when fed; never promise before you know what you are being asked.
prasangs.story_hook: The old king would have promised her anything to stop her crying, and that was exactly the problem.
prasangs.notes: Avoid the misogynist lines in Dasharatha's lament (2.12.88 etc.); frame Kaikeyi as a person manipulated by fear, not as 'women'.

prasangs.title_en: Ram accepts exile
prasangs.summary: On the morning of his coronation, Ram is summoned and told by Kaikeyi that he must go into the forest for fourteen years. He agrees without anger, and is hurt only that his father could not tell him himself. He walks out showing no change of mind, already thinking of those he must comfort.
prasangs.lesson: You cannot control the news; you can control the person who walks out of the room.
prasangs.story_hook: He went to the palace to be crowned and came out with fourteen years in the forest.
prasangs.notes: Skip 2.19.21 (absolute obedience to father).

prasangs.title_en: Kausalya lets Ram go
prasangs.summary: Ram's mother faints at the news and begs to come with him. Ram gently refuses, asks her to look after his grieving father, and wins her blessing for the journey.
prasangs.lesson: Love sometimes means staying behind to care for someone else.
prasangs.story_hook: His mother had waited seventeen years for this day, and it was taken from her in a morning.
prasangs.notes: Ram's lines on a wife's duty to her husband (2.24.10, 2.24.18) are excluded from cards.

prasangs.title_en: Lakshman's fury, Ram's calm
prasangs.summary: Lakshman is enraged by the injustice and wants to seize the throne by force. Ram calms him: set aside the insult, don't torment yourself, the setback may lead somewhere better. Lakshman answers that effort, not fate, decides; both views are given their due.
prasangs.lesson: Anger at injustice is natural; decide what to do with it before it decides for you.
prasangs.notes: Lakshman's threats (2.21.9–17, 2.23.10–28) and Ram's fatalism (2.22.13–19) are excluded from cards.

prasangs.title_en: Sita chooses to go
prasangs.summary: Ram asks Sita to stay safely in Ayodhya. She refuses, argues, laughs at his fears and insists: the hardships he lists are nothing if they face them together. Ram listens, realises he had not understood how determined she was, and agrees.
prasangs.lesson: A partnership means making big decisions together, and listening when the other has decided.
prasangs.story_hook: He came to tell her he was leaving for fourteen years; she told him she was coming.
prasangs.notes: Framed as choice and partnership; pativrata verses (2.27.4–9, 2.29.15–17) and her threats of self-harm are excluded.

prasangs.title_en: One more night: Ram leaves his father
prasangs.summary: The broken king begs Ram to stay one more night so his parents can see him. Ram gently refuses, saying a promise made must be kept and he will return in fourteen years. Dasharatha embraces him and collapses.
prasangs.lesson: Goodbyes to ageing parents are hard; leave with love and a promise to return.
prasangs.story_hook: His father asked for only one thing: one more night.

prasangs.title_en: Sumitra sends Lakshman with Ram
prasangs.summary: As the exiles leave, Lakshman's mother blesses him: treat Ram as your father, Sita as your mother, and the forest as home. She tells him to go happily.
prasangs.lesson: Home is the people you are with; you can carry it into any wilderness.
prasangs.story_hook: His mother did not ask him to stay; she told him how to make the forest home.

prasangs.title_en: Sumitra sits with Kausalya
prasangs.summary: Kausalya weeps for her son gone to the forest. Her co-queen Sumitra, whose own son has gone too, comforts her: he went for a good reason, he is not alone, and you will see him again.
prasangs.lesson: When a child leaves, a friend who shares the ache helps more than advice.
prasangs.story_hook: Two mothers, two sons gone to the same forest, and one of them found the strength to comfort the other.

prasangs.title_en: Ram slips away from the loyal crowd
prasangs.summary: Thousands of citizens follow Ram into the wilderness, determined to bring him back. At dawn he slips away while they sleep so they will go home rather than suffer for his sake.
prasangs.lesson: Leaders protect people from their troubles; they don't pull others into their own.

prasangs.title_en: Ram's messages home
prasangs.summary: The charioteer returns and delivers Ram's messages: honour our father in his old age, be kind to all three mothers including Kaikeyi. He also delivers Lakshman's furious words about their father, showing two very different ways sons respond to a parent's failure.
prasangs.lesson: Even when a parent fails you, you can choose to protect their dignity.
prasangs.story_hook: The charioteer came back alone, carrying two very different messages from two brothers.

prasangs.title_en: Kausalya's reproach and apology
prasangs.summary: In her grief Kausalya lashes out at her husband for exiling their son. When he folds his hands and asks her forgiveness, she is horrified, apologises, and explains that grief made her speak.
prasangs.lesson: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.
prasangs.story_hook: She said the words; then she saw her husband fold his hands to her.

prasangs.title_en: The boy at the river: Dasharatha's old guilt
prasangs.summary: Dying of grief, Dasharatha confesses to Kausalya that as a young prince he shot at a sound in the dark and killed a boy filling water for his blind, aged parents. He took the water to them and told them the truth himself. The father cursed him to lose a son as they had, and now, longing for Ram, the king dies at midnight.
prasangs.lesson: Carelessness can wound for decades; owning it honestly is the only way to carry it.
prasangs.story_hook: Years ago, a young prince heard a sound by the river at night and let fly an arrow.
prasangs.notes: Skip 2.63.37 (caste of the boy's parents) and 2.63.6 (karma as deserving).

prasangs.title_en: Bharata comes home too late
prasangs.summary: Bharata, living at his uncle's court, has a nightmare and is summoned home. He finds the city silent and learns from his mother that his father has died while he was away, and then that Ram is in exile because of her.
prasangs.lesson: Missing a parent's death far from home is its own grief; let yourself feel it.
prasangs.story_hook: He rode for seven days and arrived to find his father already gone.

prasangs.title_en: Bharata wrongly blamed
prasangs.summary: Bharata turns on his mother in fury. Then Ram's grieving mother assumes he plotted it all, and her words cut him like a needle in a wound. He falls at her feet and swears his innocence until she believes him.
prasangs.lesson: Being blamed for what you did not do hurts most from those you love; stay and make your truth known.
prasangs.story_hook: He had done nothing, and the one person whose good opinion he needed was sure he had done it all.
prasangs.notes: Bharata's curses on whoever approved the exile (2.75.16–) are a list of ritual sins; not for cards.

prasangs.title_en: At the pyre, and the hand that stopped
prasangs.summary: The brothers perform their father's rites and collapse in grief; the family priest lifts them up. When Shatrughna drags Manthara before him in rage, Bharata stops him: Ram would never forgive cruelty done in his name.
prasangs.lesson: Grief and rage come together; one calm person can stop a moment we'd regret forever.
prasangs.story_hook: Shatrughna had the maid by the hair when his brother's voice stopped him.
prasangs.notes: Bharata's 'a woman must not be killed' is the reason given in text; tell the restraint without the gender framing.

prasangs.title_en: Bharata refuses the throne
prasangs.summary: The court offers Bharata the kingdom his mother won for him. He refuses before the whole assembly, says it belongs to his brother, and sets out with the army and the city to bring Ram back.
prasangs.lesson: Not every gain is worth taking; integrity sometimes means refusing what you are handed.
prasangs.story_hook: Everyone expected him to take the crown; he called for his chariot instead.

prasangs.title_en: Guha's suspicion and Bharata's grief
prasangs.summary: Ram's friend Guha sees Bharata's army and assumes he has come to kill Ram. He prepares to block the river but goes to meet him first. Learning Bharata's intent, he becomes his guide and shows him the grass bed where Ram slept, where Bharata vows to live as an ascetic until Ram returns.
prasangs.lesson: Prepare if you must, but find out someone's intent before you judge them.
prasangs.story_hook: Guha saw the army coming and ordered his boats manned for battle; then he went to talk.

prasangs.title_en: Lakshman suspects Bharata
prasangs.summary: From a tree at Chitrakoot, Lakshman sees Bharata's army and is sure he has come to finish them. Ram stops him: Bharata has never wronged us; why suspect him now? And no kingdom is worth winning through wrong.
prasangs.lesson: Don't assume the worst of family on the strength of what you see from a distance.
prasangs.story_hook: Lakshman saw dust and banners on the horizon and reached for his bow.

prasangs.title_en: Ram's questions to Bharata
prasangs.summary: Meeting Bharata at Chitrakoot, Ram asks a long series of questions about how he is running the kingdom: whom he consults, how quickly he acts, whether he listens to the falsely accused.
prasangs.lesson: Good leaders consult wisely, act promptly, and listen to people with no power.
prasangs.notes: Many questions are king-only (spies, forts, treasury) and excluded.

prasangs.title_en: The brothers meet at Chitrakoot
prasangs.summary: Bharata finds Ram in bark clothes and falls weeping at his feet, blaming himself. Ram embraces him, tells him he sees no fault in him, and asks him not to blame his mother. Then Ram learns their father is dead and grieves that he was not there.
prasangs.lesson: A rift can close in one embrace; grief shared between siblings is lighter.
prasangs.story_hook: Bharata saw his brother in bark and matted hair, and could not get past the word 'brother'.

prasangs.title_en: Ram on why grief must not rule us
prasangs.summary: Bharata begs Ram to return and rule. Ram answers with a teaching on impermanence: everything gathered runs out, everything rising falls, people meet like logs on the ocean and drift apart. Grieve, but do not let grief overturn your duty.
prasangs.lesson: Everything that comes together parts; let that make you gentler, not hopeless.

prasangs.title_en: Jabali's doubt
prasangs.summary: The priest Jabali argues that nobody belongs to anyone, rituals are empty and only the present matters, so Ram should take the throne. Ram answers that conduct, not claims, shows who we are, and that people follow the example of those who lead.
prasangs.lesson: Doubt deserves a hearing; answer it with how you choose to live.
prasangs.notes: Ram's anti-Buddhist/atheist line (2.109.33) excluded. Jabali's view is given fairly as a serious challenge.

prasangs.title_en: The sandals: a compromise between brothers
prasangs.summary: Bharata threatens to fast at Ram's door until he returns. Ram persuades him to rise, and they reach a compromise: Bharata takes Ram's sandals to rule in his name. At parting Ram asks him to drop his resentment of their mother.
prasangs.lesson: When neither can give way, find a form that honours both; and let go of blame.
prasangs.story_hook: Neither brother would give way, so Bharata asked for his brother's sandals.

prasangs.title_en: Bharata's fourteen years at Nandigram
prasangs.summary: Bharata refuses to live in the palace. From a village hut he governs in the name of Ram's sandals, dressed as an ascetic, holding everything in trust and waiting fourteen years for his brother.
prasangs.lesson: Waiting can be active: keep faith by taking care of what was entrusted to you.
prasangs.story_hook: For fourteen years the king of Ayodhya was a pair of wooden sandals.

prasangs.title_en: Sita questions the weapon
prasangs.summary: Sita worries that Ram, carrying weapons among peaceful hermits, will be drawn into needless violence. She tells the story of a hermit changed by keeping a sword. Ram thanks her, saying no one advises a person they don't care about, and explains his promise to protect the sages.
prasangs.lesson: Disagree with someone you love openly; advice is a sign of care.

prasangs.title_en: Maricha warns Ravana
prasangs.summary: Ravana asks Maricha to help him abduct Sita. Maricha, who has met Ram before, warns him again and again: flatterers are many, truth-tellers rare, and those heading for a fall reject good advice. Ravana threatens him until he agrees.
prasangs.lesson: Listen hardest to the advice you least want to hear.
prasangs.story_hook: Maricha had met Ram once before and barely lived; now his king wanted him to do it again.

prasangs.title_en: The golden deer
prasangs.summary: A dazzling deer with a golden, jewelled hide appears near the hut. Lakshman warns that no such deer exists; it must be a trick. Sita longs for it and Ram, captivated too, gives chase, leaving the hut exposed.
prasangs.lesson: When something looks too perfect to be real, pause before you chase it.
prasangs.story_hook: It was the most beautiful animal anyone had ever seen, and that should have been the warning.
prasangs.notes: Sita's harsh words to Lakshman (3.45) are excluded: the passage turns into Lakshman's misogynist reply.

prasangs.title_en: Jatayu, old and brave
prasangs.summary: The aged vulture Jatayu wakes to see Ravana carrying Sita off. He warns him, then fights him alone and is mortally wounded. Later Ram finds him dying, hears his news, and cremates him with the honour due a father.
prasangs.lesson: Age is no reason to stop standing up for what's right; honour those who stood up for you.
prasangs.story_hook: He was sixty thousand years old, and he flew straight at the ten-headed king.
prasangs.notes: Range spans the fight (3.50–3.51) and Ram's farewell (3.67–3.68); the sargas between are other episodes. Tagged pet_loss as the nearest fit: Ram mourns an animal companion with full funeral honours.

prasangs.title_en: Ram's grief and Lakshman's counsel
prasangs.summary: Ram returns to an empty hut. He searches, questions trees and animals, breaks down and finally rages that he will destroy the world. Lakshman calms him: don't punish the whole world for one person's crime; trouble comes to everyone and passes.
prasangs.lesson: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.
prasangs.story_hook: He came back to the hut calling her name, and no one answered.
prasangs.notes: Sarga 3.58 is empty in our data.

prasangs.title_en: Kabandha: find a friend who understands
prasangs.summary: Freed from a curse, the creature Kabandha tells the grieving brothers to seek out Sugriva, an exile who has also lost his wife and home. Only a friend in the same trouble, he says, can help them now.
prasangs.lesson: When you are lost, look for someone who has been through the same thing.
prasangs.story_hook: Rising from his own funeral pyre, the strange creature gave the brothers one piece of advice.

prasangs.title_en: Shabari's long wait
prasangs.summary: The old ascetic woman Shabari has lived for years at Pampa after her teachers died, told that Ram would one day come. She has kept gathering forest food for him. When he arrives, she welcomes him, shows him her teachers' forest, and departs in peace.
prasangs.lesson: Faithful waiting, unseen by the world, is not wasted.
prasangs.story_hook: Her teachers had all gone, and still she gathered fruit every day for a guest who had never come.
prasangs.notes: Valmiki does not have the tasted-berries story; do not add it.

prasangs.title_en: Grief in springtime at Pampa
prasangs.summary: At the beautiful lake of Pampa in spring, everything reminds Ram of Sita and his grief deepens. Lakshman tells him there is no strength greater than enthusiasm, and to rouse himself.
prasangs.lesson: Beauty can sharpen grief; a friend can remind you of your own strength.
prasangs.story_hook: Spring had come to the lake, and every flower made Ram's grief worse.

prasangs.title_en: Sugriva's fear and Hanuman's first words
prasangs.summary: The exiled Sugriva sees two armed strangers and panics, sure his brother has sent assassins. Hanuman calms him and goes in disguise to find out. His speech to the brothers is so clear and gentle that Ram is moved and trusts him at once.
prasangs.lesson: Fear jumps ahead of facts; calm, clear words build trust fast.
prasangs.story_hook: Sugriva saw two archers walking towards his hill and was sure they had come to kill him.

prasangs.title_en: Ram and Sugriva's friendship
prasangs.summary: Ram and Sugriva swear friendship before a fire. Sugriva shows Ram the jewels Sita dropped; Ram breaks down, and Sugriva comforts him: in trouble the steady person thinks it through, and a friend is the greatest refuge.
prasangs.lesson: Two people in trouble can carry each other.
prasangs.story_hook: Two exiles, each robbed of his wife and home, swore friendship over a fire.

prasangs.title_en: The cave: how two brothers fell apart
prasangs.summary: Vali chases a demon into a cave and tells Sugriva to wait. A year later blood flows out and no voice answers; Sugriva seals the cave in grief and is made king. Vali escapes, believes he was betrayed, and refuses every apology, driving Sugriva out.
prasangs.lesson: Many family rifts start with a misunderstanding neither side stops to check.
prasangs.story_hook: He waited at the mouth of the cave for a whole year, and then he saw the blood.

prasangs.title_en: Tara's warning
prasangs.summary: Sugriva roars a second challenge and Vali storms out to fight. His wife Tara stops him: drop this anger, fight tomorrow if you must, make peace with your brother, who is your own family. Vali will not listen.
prasangs.lesson: Anger rushes; good counsel says wait until morning, and remember who family is.
prasangs.story_hook: Vali was already at the door when Tara caught his arm.

prasangs.title_en: Vali's last words
prasangs.summary: Struck down by Ram's arrow during the duel, Vali rebukes Ram, then makes his peace. To Sugriva he says: don't hold my faults against me; we could not have both brotherhood and kingdom. He entrusts his son to his brother and tells Angada how to live.
prasangs.lesson: Rivalry seems huge until the end; then only the relationship matters.
prasangs.story_hook: Lying on the ground, the brother who had driven him out asked him for forgiveness.
prasangs.notes: The Ram–Vali debate on the killing (4.17–4.18) is excluded from cards; tell the episode through the brothers.

prasangs.title_en: Sugriva's remorse
prasangs.summary: Sugriva has won, but seeing Tara's grief he is crushed by remorse: how could anyone enjoy a kingdom bought with a brother's life? He remembers Vali only ever said 'don't do it again.'
prasangs.lesson: Winning against family rarely feels like winning.
prasangs.story_hook: He had the crown at last, and could not bear to look at it.
prasangs.notes: His wish to die (4.24.22–23) and Tara's death wish are not for cards.

prasangs.title_en: Waiting out the monsoon
prasangs.summary: The rains come and Ram must wait four months on a mountain before any search can begin. He cannot sleep for grief. Lakshman reminds him that endless grieving drains every purpose, and that this is a season for waiting. Ram resolves to wait and to give Sugriva time.
prasangs.lesson: Some seasons are for waiting; wait well, without letting grief take you.
prasangs.story_hook: The rains came, and with them four months in which nothing at all could be done.

prasangs.title_en: Sugriva forgets his promise
prasangs.summary: Restored to his throne, Sugriva sinks into pleasure and forgets his promise to search for Sita. Hanuman warns him that help given late counts for little. Autumn comes; angry, Ram sends Lakshman, and Hanuman counsels the frightened Sugriva to bear harsh words and keep faith.
prasangs.lesson: Comfort makes us forget our promises; a true friend reminds us in time.
prasangs.story_hook: The rains ended, the roads dried, and the king who had promised everything was still at his party.

prasangs.title_en: Tara calms Lakshman
prasangs.summary: Lakshman storms into Kishkindha, bow twanging. Tara meets him with reason and courtesy: strong people think before anger takes over; bear the slip of someone on your side. Sugriva apologises and Lakshman asks forgiveness for his own harsh words.
prasangs.lesson: A calm voice can turn a confrontation into an apology on both sides.
prasangs.story_hook: Lakshman came through the gates ready to fight, and found a woman standing in his way.
prasangs.notes: Lakshman's 'ingrates deserve death' (4.34.9–11) is excluded.

prasangs.title_en: The missed deadline
prasangs.summary: The southern search party loses time in a magic cave and misses Sugriva's deadline. Angada rallies them once, then despairs, fearing punishment and certain he will be blamed. Hanuman reasons with him to return.
prasangs.lesson: Missing a deadline feels final; it rarely is.
prasangs.story_hook: They came out of the cave to find that spring had already come, and their deadline had gone.
prasangs.notes: The resolve to fast unto death (4.53, 4.55) is not for cards; retell without dwelling on it.

prasangs.title_en: Sampati, the bird who could not fly
prasangs.summary: The despairing monkeys meet Sampati, Jatayu's old brother, whose wings burnt long ago. A sage once told him to live on, because one day his knowledge would be needed. Now he tells them Sita is in Lanka, and his wings grow back.
prasangs.lesson: Even when you feel useless, your experience may be exactly what someone needs.
prasangs.story_hook: For thousands of years the old bird had sat on a mountain with no wings, waiting for a reason.
prasangs.notes: Sampati's thoughts of ending his life (4.63.4–5) are not for cards.

prasangs.title_en: Jambavan reminds Hanuman who he is
prasangs.summary: At the ocean's edge, each monkey says how far he can leap; none can cross. Old Jambavan turns to Hanuman, who has sat silent, and reminds him of his birth and power: why are you holding back? This is your time. Hanuman grows and prepares to leap.
prasangs.lesson: Sometimes you need someone to remind you what you are capable of.
prasangs.story_hook: Everyone had named a number, and the one who could actually do it was sitting quietly at the back.

prasangs.title_en: Hanuman's leap
prasangs.summary: Hanuman leaps across the ocean. A mountain rises to repay an old kindness by offering rest; he thanks it but keeps his promise not to stop. He outwits Surasa by shrinking small and defeats Simhika, and the watching beings praise his steadiness, sight, judgement and skill.
prasangs.lesson: Gratitude and focus can go together; know when to be big and when to be small.
prasangs.story_hook: Halfway across the ocean, a golden mountain rose out of the water and offered him a place to rest.

prasangs.title_en: Hanuman's search and near despair
prasangs.summary: Hanuman searches Lanka all night without finding Sita. He is close to despair, weighing what failure will mean for everyone, then tells himself that refusing to lose heart is the root of success, and searches again.
prasangs.lesson: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.
prasangs.story_hook: Hanuman had searched every palace in Lanka by moonlight, and she was nowhere.
prasangs.notes: 5.13.33–39 (thoughts of death) not for cards.

prasangs.title_en: Sita refuses Ravana
prasangs.summary: Ravana comes to the grove offering Sita wealth and power, and threatens her with death if she refuses. Trembling, she places a blade of grass between them and refuses: she cannot be bought, and he should return her before he destroys himself.
prasangs.lesson: Power and money cannot buy what you refuse to sell.
prasangs.story_hook: She had no weapon, so she put a blade of grass between herself and the king of Lanka.
prasangs.notes: Avoid the pativrata lines (5.21.4–5, 5.21.16).

prasangs.title_en: Sita in captivity
prasangs.summary: Guards threaten Sita day and night. She fears Ram has forgotten her, then reminds herself that out of sight is out of mind only for the ungrateful. The guard Trijata dreams of Ram's victory, and good omens begin to appear.
prasangs.lesson: Hold on to love across distance; hope can arrive from unexpected people.
prasangs.story_hook: She had been alone in the grove for ten months, surrounded by guards who mocked her every day.
prasangs.notes: 5.28 contains Sita's thoughts of ending her life; retell with care or skip that part.

prasangs.title_en: How Hanuman spoke to Sita
prasangs.summary: Hanuman has found Sita but she is terrified. He thinks carefully: speak in ordinary language, not court Sanskrit; don't gamble on a fight; start by gently praising Ram so she can trust him. He sings Ram's story softly from the tree, and she hears hope for the first time: joy comes to the one who stays alive.
prasangs.lesson: Before a hard conversation, think about how the other person will hear you.
prasangs.story_hook: He had found her at last, and now the problem was how to speak without making her scream.

prasangs.title_en: Hanuman's anger and the burning of Lanka
prasangs.summary: Hanuman decides to test the enemy, smashes a grove, is captured and has his tail set on fire. He burns the city in fury, then is horrified that Sita might have died in the fire: in anger, he says, he nearly wrecked the very thing he came to do.
prasangs.lesson: Anger can win a small fight and ruin the real goal.
prasangs.story_hook: The city was burning behind him, and then a terrible thought stopped him cold.
prasangs.notes: 5.55.6 is truncated in data.

prasangs.title_en: Ram thanks Hanuman
prasangs.summary: Hanuman returns with Sita's jewel and her message. Ram is overwhelmed: Hanuman has saved them all, and Ram, an exile, has nothing to give in return, so he embraces him.
prasangs.lesson: When you can't repay a kindness, give what you have: thanks, and your heart.
prasangs.story_hook: Hanuman had crossed an ocean and back; Ram, an exile, had nothing to give him.

prasangs.title_en: Vibhishana tells his brother the truth
prasangs.summary: In Ravana's war council, everyone else flatters him. Vibhishana alone says what he has seen: return Sita, avoid war. Ravana insults him as a traitor. Vibhishana says flatterers are easy to find and truth-tellers rare, wishes his brother well, and leaves.
prasangs.lesson: Speak the truth to family even when it costs you; leave if you must, without hatred.
prasangs.story_hook: Everyone in the hall agreed with the king, except his youngest brother.
prasangs.notes: Ravana's sharp aphorisms (6.16.2–14) serve his attack and are excluded.

prasangs.title_en: Ram takes in the enemy's brother
prasangs.summary: Vibhishana arrives at Ram's camp. The allies suspect a spy; Hanuman reads him as sincere. Ram decides: he will not turn away anyone who comes in friendship, even with faults; whoever comes once and says 'I am yours' he will protect.
prasangs.lesson: Give a second chance to someone who comes to you sincerely, even across old lines.
prasangs.story_hook: The enemy king's own brother was standing at the edge of the camp, asking to come in.

prasangs.title_en: Building the bridge
prasangs.summary: Ram waits three days for the ocean to let him pass, then loses patience. The ocean reveals that Nala can build a bridge; Nala admits his skill and the whole army hauls trees and rocks for five days until the bridge reaches Lanka.
prasangs.lesson: Big things get built by many hands, once someone admits they know how.
prasangs.story_hook: The army stood on the shore with no boats, until a quiet monkey said he knew how to build a bridge.
prasangs.notes: The squirrel story is not in Valmiki; do not add it. The ocean episode before it is vr.p.ocean_humility_firmness.

prasangs.title_en: Sarama, a friend in the enemy's house
prasangs.summary: Ravana tries to break Sita with a fake head of Ram. Sarama, a kind rakshasi guard, comforts her, tells her the truth, and offers to find out what is being planned. Sita asks only to be told whatever is decided.
prasangs.lesson: One kind person can make an unbearable place bearable; knowing is easier than wondering.
prasangs.story_hook: Among all the guards, one of them wiped Sita's tears and told her the truth.

prasangs.title_en: Ram lets Ravana go to rest
prasangs.summary: In their first fight, Ram shatters Ravana's chariot, bow and crown. Instead of killing his exhausted enemy he tells him to go home, rest and come back. Ravana goes back to Lanka humbled, his pride broken.
prasangs.lesson: Real strength can afford to be generous; pride is what breaks a person.
prasangs.story_hook: Ravana stood without a bow or a crown, waiting for the final arrow, and Ram told him to go home.

prasangs.title_en: Kumbhakarna's loyalty
prasangs.summary: Woken from months of sleep, Kumbhakarna tells Ravana bluntly that his pride caused this disaster and he acted in the wrong order. Then, loyal to his brother, he goes out to fight anyway, scorning boastful courtiers: the brave don't praise themselves, they act.
prasangs.lesson: You can tell family the hard truth and still stand by them; humility does, boasting talks.
prasangs.story_hook: The giant woke after nine months asleep and told his brother exactly what he had done wrong.
prasangs.notes: Fighting for a brother he knows is wrong is presented as a dilemma, not an ideal.

prasangs.title_en: Lakshman struck down
prasangs.summary: Ravana's spear fells Lakshman. Ram breaks down: even victory means nothing without his brother, who comforted him in every low moment. The physician Sushena sees Lakshman still breathes and sends Hanuman for the healing herbs; Hanuman brings back the mountain peak.
prasangs.lesson: When someone you love is gravely ill, remember what they mean to you, and do what can be done.
prasangs.story_hook: Ram knelt over his brother in the dust and forgot there was a battle going on.
prasangs.notes: Skip 6.101.11 ('wives can be found in every land').

prasangs.title_en: Vibhishana mourns Ravana
prasangs.summary: Ravana is dead. Vibhishana weeps for the brother who drove him out and hesitates to perform his rites. Ram tells him enmity ends at death and Ravana is now his to honour. Mandodari mourns: once he mastered his desires and won the world; in the end his desires mastered him.
prasangs.lesson: Grief for someone who wronged you is real; death ends the fight.
prasangs.story_hook: The war was won, and the man who had switched sides sat down by his brother's body and wept.

prasangs.title_en: Sita spares her guards
prasangs.summary: Hanuman brings Sita the news of victory and offers to punish the guards who tormented her. She refuses: they were following orders, and no one is without fault; show compassion even to those who wronged you.
prasangs.lesson: Mercy toward those who hurt you is a strength, not a weakness.
prasangs.story_hook: For months the guards had tormented her; now Hanuman asked her permission to punish them.
prasangs.notes: Hanuman's proposed tortures (6.113.21–23) and Sita's karma line (6.113.25) excluded.

prasangs.title_en: Sita answers unjust suspicion
prasangs.summary: After the war Ram publicly doubts Sita. She answers with dignity: why speak to me like a stranger? After all our years together, if you don't know me, that loss is permanent. She then walks into fire to prove what should not have needed proof.
prasangs.lesson: Being doubted by someone close is a deep injustice; you are allowed to name it.
prasangs.notes: Framed as injustice and grief; the test is not endorsed. Keep out of daily feeds unless the user's situation is suspicion or mistrust.

prasangs.title_en: Ram hurries home
prasangs.summary: Victorious, Ram refuses Lanka's honours: his heart is in a hurry to see Bharata. Near Ayodhya he sends Hanuman ahead to read Bharata's face, saying if Bharata now wants the kingdom, let him keep it.
prasangs.lesson: Homecoming is about people, not possessions; don't let property come between siblings.
prasangs.story_hook: He had won the war and Lanka was his to enjoy, but all he wanted was to see his brother.

prasangs.title_en: Bharata's fourteen-year wait ends
prasangs.summary: Hanuman finds Bharata thin, in bark clothes, still waiting. Hearing Ram is near, Bharata faints with joy: a person who stays alive will find joy, even after a hundred years. He places the sandals back on Ram's feet and hands back the kingdom he kept in trust, now ten times richer.
prasangs.lesson: Faithful waiting is rewarded; return what was entrusted to you, and more.
prasangs.story_hook: For fourteen years Bharata had counted the days; now a stranger was telling him to stop.
prasangs.notes: 6.126.2 repeats Sita's 5.34.5 (joy comes to the living), already curated.

prasangs.title_en: Ram takes his brother's advice
prasangs.summary: Ram proposes a great imperial sacrifice. Bharata gently objects that it would bring suffering to many kings and people. Ram listens and changes course, saying good advice should be taken even from the young.
prasangs.lesson: Leaders who change their minds on good advice earn more trust, not less.
prasangs.story_hook: The emperor proposed a grand plan, and his younger brother quietly said no.

prasangs.title_en: King Nriga and the petitioners who waited
prasangs.summary: After four days of neglecting his work, Ram calls in everyone waiting, and tells of King Nriga: two men brought him a dispute, waited for days at his gate and were never admitted, and their anger cost him dearly.
prasangs.lesson: Delay is a decision too; people waiting on you are paying for it.
prasangs.story_hook: Two men waited at a king's gate for days, and no one let them in.
prasangs.notes: The curse framing and gift-to-brahmins details are background only.

prasangs.title_en: Sita left in the forest
prasangs.summary: Hearing that people gossip about Sita's time in Lanka, Ram orders Lakshman to leave her, pregnant, near Valmiki's hermitage. Lakshman obeys in anguish. Sita grieves that she is cut off from everyone and slandered though innocent. Valmiki finds her, says he knows she is blameless, and tells her to treat his home as her own.
prasangs.lesson: Injustice from those we love is real grief; a stranger's kindness can become home.
prasangs.story_hook: Lakshman stopped the chariot at the river and could not bring himself to say why.
prasangs.notes: Framed as grief and injustice; the abandonment is not endorsed. Skip 7.45.10–12 (Ram on reputation) and 7.48.15 (husband as god).

prasangs.title_en: Sita refuses to prove herself again
prasangs.summary: Years later, Valmiki brings Sita before Ram's assembly. Ram admits he knew she was innocent but gave in to gossip, and asks her to swear her purity once more. Sita calls on the earth instead, and the earth takes her back; she does not return.
prasangs.lesson: There is a point where you stop proving yourself to people who will not believe you.
prasangs.story_hook: She had proved herself once in fire; when they asked her to prove it again, she chose to leave.
prasangs.notes: Framed as Sita's dignity and refusal; Ram's admission (7.97.4) is an admission of wrong, not a justification.

prasangs.title_en: Tulsidas on good company and difficult people
prasangs.title_hi: ब्राह्मण-संत वंदना; खल वंदना; संत-असंत वंदना
prasangs.summary: Before the story begins, Tulsidas bows to good people and, with gentle irony, to troublesome ones too. He describes how each acts, why company shapes us, and how the wise take the good and leave the rest, like the swan taking milk from water.
prasangs.lesson: The people around you shape your judgement; choose them, and take the good from everyone.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 3, 4, 5 (raw_json order range 19-60; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units). Opening invocations; teaching, not story.

prasangs.title_en: Tulsidas on loving our own work
prasangs.title_hi: तुलसीदासजी की दीनता और राम भक्तिमयी कविता की महिमा
prasangs.summary: Tulsidas calls his own poetry plain and asks readers to forgive it. Along the way he notes that everyone loves their own work, that few are glad at another's success, and that most people swell only with their own rising waters.
prasangs.lesson: Notice whether you can be glad at someone else's good work, not only your own.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 6 (raw_json order range 61-102; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units).

prasangs.title_en: Sati doubts, tests and hides it
prasangs.title_hi: सती का भ्रम, श्री रामजी का ऐश्वर्य और सती का खेद; शिवजी द्वारा सती का त्याग, शिवजी की समाधि
prasangs.summary: Sati sees Shiva bow to Ram, a grieving prince searching the forest, and cannot believe Ram is divine. Ignoring Shiva's advice, she tests Ram by taking Sita's form, is found out, and then lies to Shiva about it. Shiva quietly withdraws from her, and she lives with a guilt she cannot speak.
prasangs.lesson: Doubt can be honest; hiding what you did is what breaks trust.
prasangs.story_hook: Sati watched her husband bow to a weeping stranger in the forest, and she did not believe what she saw.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 15, 16 (raw_json order range 301-369; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units). Shiva's line 1.48.chaupai.8 ('what is meant to happen will happen') was dropped earlier for fatalism; tell the story without it.

prasangs.title_en: Sati goes to her father's sacrifice uninvited
prasangs.title_hi: सती का दक्ष यज्ञ में जाना; पति के अपमान से दुःखी होकर सती का योगाग्नि से जल जाना, दक्ष यज्ञ विध्वंस
prasangs.summary: Sati's father Daksha holds a great sacrifice and invites everyone except Shiva and her. Shiva warns her that going where there is hostility brings no good, but she goes. Her father ignores her and insults her husband in front of everyone, and the visit ends in catastrophe.
prasangs.lesson: You may go to family without an invitation, but not into open hostility; listen to that warning.
prasangs.story_hook: The sky over Kailash filled with chariots heading to her father's feast, and none of them had come for her.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 17, 18 (raw_json order range 370-392; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units). The episode ends with Sati giving up her body in yogic fire (1.60). For a 150-word retelling, end at the insult and say only that it ended in tragedy; avoid presenting self-immolation as a response.

prasangs.title_en: Parvati holds to her choice
prasangs.title_hi: पार्वती का जन्म और तपस्या; सप्तर्षियों की परीक्षा में पार्वतीजी का महत्व
prasangs.summary: Reborn as Parvati, Sati resolves to marry Shiva and spends years in austerity. The seven sages come to test her, mocking Shiva as a homeless ascetic and offering her a better match. She answers that gold keeps its nature even in fire, and that the heart wants the one it has chosen.
prasangs.lesson: Persistence is choosing the same thing again each day, even when others call it foolish.
prasangs.story_hook: The sages came to talk Parvati out of it, and they listed every flaw in the man she had chosen.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 19, 21 (raw_json order range 393-484; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units). Range spans prasangs 19 and 21 (20, Ram's request to Shiva, sits between). Avoid 1.75 doha (sages' remark about women in an ascetic's house).

prasangs.title_en: Narada's pride and the monkey face
prasangs.title_hi: नारद का अभिमान और माया का प्रभाव; विश्वमोहिनी का स्वयंवर, शिवगणों तथा भगवान्‌ को शाप और नारद का मोहभंग
prasangs.summary: Narada conquers desire in meditation and cannot stop telling people about it. Vishnu creates a city and a princess's swayamvara; Narada falls for her and asks Vishnu for a beautiful face. Vishnu, like a doctor refusing harmful food, gives him a monkey's face instead, and Narada is laughed out of the hall until he sees what his pride has done.
prasangs.lesson: The moment you boast of beating a weakness, it has found another way in.
prasangs.story_hook: Narada had conquered desire, and that was the problem: he could not stop talking about it.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 29, 30 (raw_json order range 724-793; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units). Narada's curse on Vishnu includes 'you will suffer separation from a woman' (1.131.4); fine in retelling. 1.123.chaupai.2 (seed of pride) is a usable second anchor if wanted.

prasangs.title_en: Manu and Shatarupa ask late in life
prasangs.summary: King Manu and Queen Shatarupa realise in old age that a whole life has passed without what mattered most to them. They hand over the kingdom, go to the forest and practise austerity for years. When Vishnu offers a boon, Manu hesitates like a poor man before the wishing tree, then asks for a son like God himself.
prasangs.lesson: It is not too late to turn towards what matters, but it takes courage to ask for it.
prasangs.story_hook: The king had ruled well for a lifetime, and one morning he realised he had missed the point.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 31 (raw_json order range 794-849; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units).

prasangs.title_en: Kausalya and the child who ran from dinner
prasangs.title_hi: श्री भगवान्‌ का प्राकट्य और बाललीला का आनंद
prasangs.summary: At his birth Ram shows Kausalya his cosmic form, and she asks him instead to be simply a baby. Later scenes are pure childhood: the boy runs off mid-meal, curd on his face, dusty from play, while his father laughs and his mother chases him. When she once glimpses the whole universe in him again, she asks only to be spared that and keep her child.
prasangs.lesson: The grandest thing about a child may be the ordinary hours of childhood itself.
prasangs.story_hook: Kausalya was shown the whole universe in her newborn, and all she wanted was for him to cry like a baby.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 37 (raw_json order range 1049-1126; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units).

prasangs.title_en: Dasharath lets his sons go
prasangs.title_hi: विश्वामित्र का राजा दशरथ से राम-लक्ष्मण को माँगना, ताड़का वध
prasangs.summary: The sage Vishwamitra asks King Dasharath to send the teenage Ram and Lakshman to protect his forest rites from demons. Dasharath, who had his sons late in life, offers land, cows, treasure, even his own life instead. Vasishtha reasons with him, and he finally embraces the boys and hands them over.
prasangs.lesson: Parents protect children best by letting them go when the time comes.
prasangs.story_hook: The king offered the sage his treasury, his kingdom, even his own life, anything but his sons.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 38 (raw_json order range 1127-1149; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units).

prasangs.title_en: Janaka's despair and the bow
prasangs.title_hi: बंदीजनों द्वारा जनकप्रतिज्ञा की घोषणा राजाओं से धनुष न उठना, जनक की निराशाजनक वाणी; श्री लक्ष्मणजी का क्रोध
prasangs.summary: Ten thousand kings fail to lift Shiva's bow, and Janaka cries out that the earth has no heroes left. Lakshman bristles; Vishwamitra sends Ram forward. Ram sees Sita's anguish, knows that rain after the crops have dried is useless, lifts the bow and breaks it in a moment.
prasangs.lesson: Some moments do not wait; when it is time, act.
prasangs.story_hook: Ten thousand kings had tried the bow, and the room had gone quiet.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 47, 48 (raw_json order range 1353-1419; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units). Kept because of 1.247 (timing). Avoid 1.237.chaupai.1 simile about women and lust.

prasangs.title_en: Parashurama's rage, Lakshman's taunts, Ram's calm
prasangs.title_hi: जयमाला पहनाना, परशुराम का आगमन व क्रोध; श्री राम-लक्ष्मण और परशुराम-संवाद
prasangs.summary: Parashurama storms into the wedding hall furious that Shiva's bow is broken. Lakshman answers every threat with a joke, and each reply feeds the fire. Ram steps in with soft words, takes the blame on himself, and calmly points out that an old bow broke at a touch; the sage's anger finally turns to recognition.
prasangs.lesson: Clever replies feed anger; calm, humble words put it out.
prasangs.story_hook: The bow was already broken, and the man who had come to avenge it was carrying an axe.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 49, 50 (raw_json order range 1420-1539; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units). Parashurama's boasts about killing kshatriyas and unborn children (1.256.4, 1.263 doha) should be left out of retellings.

prasangs.title_en: Janaka says goodbye to his daughter
prasangs.summary: After the wedding the time comes for Sita to leave Mithila. The palace, even the pet parrots, are in tears. Janaka, known everywhere for his detachment, holds his daughter and loses all composure; his ministers have to remind him it is time.
prasangs.lesson: Even the wisest parent breaks a little when a child leaves home; that is love.
prasangs.story_hook: He was the most detached king in the world, and his daughter was leaving.
prasangs.notes: Own sub-range. Sub-range of prasang 53 (1.313-1.320). Leave out the mothers' and father's advice on wifely duty (1.315.3, 1.319.1).

prasangs.title_en: Ram's unease on the eve of his crowning
prasangs.summary: Dasharath, noticing grey hairs, decides to crown Ram heir, and the whole city celebrates. When Vasishtha brings Ram the news, Ram's first thought is not joy but unease: the brothers were born, raised and married together, so why should only the eldest be crowned?
prasangs.lesson: Real affection for siblings feels uneasy when one is favoured over the rest.
prasangs.story_hook: The whole city was celebrating his coronation, and Ram was thinking about his brothers.
prasangs.notes: Own sub-range. First part of prasang 56.

prasangs.title_en: Manthara poisons Kaikeyi's mind
prasangs.title_hi: सरस्वती का मन्थरा की बुद्धि फेरना, कैकेयी-मन्थरा संवाद, प्रजा में खुशी; कैकेयी का कोपभवन में जाना
prasangs.summary: Kaikeyi is first delighted that Ram will be crowned; she loves him like her own son. Her maid Manthara works on her slowly, with sighs, hints and sweet-sounding fears about her future, until Kaikeyi believes her enemy is her only friend and goes to the sulking chamber to demand her two boons.
prasangs.lesson: Advice that flatters your fears can turn a good heart; check who benefits from it.
prasangs.story_hook: Kaikeyi was happy for Ram until her maid started to cry.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 57, 58 (raw_json order range 2011-2075; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units). The text mocks Manthara's body and uses lines on 'women's nature' (2.14.3, 2.15 doha, 2.17 doha, 2.27.4). Leave these out; tell it as manipulation, not as a story about women.

prasangs.title_en: Dasharath's two promises
prasangs.title_hi: दशरथ-कैकेयी संवाद और दशरथ शोक, सुमन्त्र का महल में जाना और वहाँ से लौटकर श्री रामजी को महल में भेजना
prasangs.summary: Dasharath finds Kaikeyi in the sulking chamber and, eager to please her, swears by Ram to grant anything. She asks for Bharat's coronation and fourteen years of exile for Ram. Bound by his word and his love, the king spends the night begging, raging and grieving, and by morning cannot speak.
prasangs.lesson: Promise only what you have thought through; a rash vow can cost what you love most.
prasangs.story_hook: He swore by the person he loved most before he knew what she would ask.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 59 (raw_json order range 2076-2149; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units). Anchor is the Chitrakoot line 'think before you act' from the existing set. Raghukul riti (2.28.2) was dropped earlier because it is spoken while making the rash promise.

prasangs.title_en: Ram hears he is to be exiled
prasangs.summary: Ram is called to his father's room and finds him collapsed. Kaikeyi tells him the terms. Ram smiles: his brother gets the throne, he gets to meet sages in the forest, and he can keep his father's word. Kaikeyi reads his plain words as cunning, and Ram walks out feeling, the poet says, like an elephant freed from its post.
prasangs.lesson: A lost role can be met with grace; sometimes it even feels like freedom.
prasangs.story_hook: Ram walked in expecting a crown and walked out with a forest.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 60 (raw_json order range 2150-2207; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units). 2.41.chaupai.4 ('blessed is the son devoted to parents') needs a misuse line if used; not selected.

prasangs.title_en: Kausalya lets her son go
prasangs.title_hi: श्री राम-कौसल्या संवाद; श्री राम-कौसल्या-सीता संवाद
prasangs.summary: Ram comes to his mother as she is preparing for his coronation. Torn between duty and love, she decides not to hold him back with 'false affection', blesses him and asks only that he not forget her. As he leaves she wonders aloud whether she will live to see his face again.
prasangs.lesson: Letting a child go with your blessing is love at its hardest.
prasangs.story_hook: She had the sweets ready for his coronation when he came to say goodbye.
prasangs.notes: Own sub-range. Prasangs 61 and 63; the Sita-Ram dialogue (62) between them is skipped (wifely-duty content).

prasangs.title_en: Sumitra sends Lakshman with Ram
prasangs.title_hi: श्री राम-लक्ष्मण संवाद; श्री लक्ष्मण-सुमित्रा संवाद
prasangs.summary: Ram asks Lakshman to stay and care for their old father and grieving mothers; Lakshman cannot imagine life apart from him. He goes to his mother Sumitra, afraid she will stop him. Instead she tells him that home is wherever Ram is, as day is wherever the sun shines, and gives him one piece of advice for the road.
prasangs.lesson: Home is where your people are; a good send-off gives values, not just tears.
prasangs.story_hook: Lakshman went to his mother expecting to be told to stay.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 64, 65 (raw_json order range 2300-2333; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units). Avoid 2.74.chaupai.1 (better barren than mother of a son who turns from Ram).

prasangs.title_en: Lakshman and Guha by the sleeping Ram
prasangs.title_hi: श्री राम का श्रृंगवेरपुर पहुँचना, निषाद के द्वारा सेवा; लक्ष्मण-निषाद संवाद, श्री राम-सीता से सुमन्त्र का संवाद, सुमंत्र का लौटना
prasangs.summary: On the first night of exile, Guha the boatmen's chief sees Ram and Sita sleeping on grass and weeps with anger at Kaikeyi. Lakshman, keeping watch, tells him no one gives us joy or sorrow; we live out our own actions, so don't blame anyone needlessly.
prasangs.lesson: Before blaming someone for your pain, look at the whole chain of causes, including yourself.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press-style prasang(s) 68, 69 (raw_json order range 2390-2450; ids approximate, the data order is offset by a few units). Includes the 'Lakshman Gita' on the world as a dream (2.90.3-2.91.4), too abstract for cards.

prasangs.title_en: Kevat washes Ram's feet
prasangs.title_hi: केवट का प्रेम और गंगा पार जाना
prasangs.summary: At the Ganga, a boatman refuses to take Ram across until he can wash his feet, joking that if the dust of those feet turned a stone into a woman, it might turn his boat, his family's livelihood, into one too. Ram laughs and agrees. On the far bank Sita offers her ring as fare, and Kevat refuses: after a lifetime of wages, today he has been paid in full.
prasangs.lesson: Some exchanges can't be priced; gratitude can be payment enough.
prasangs.story_hook: The boatman would not let the prince into his boat until he had washed his feet.
