prasangs.summary: The day before sailing for England, he sends a young doctor starting a magazine a few lines: go on bravely, don't expect success in a day or a year, hold to the highest, avoid jealousy. He tells him to reread them whenever worry or jealousy returns.
prasangs.lesson: Expect slow success, stay steady, and drop jealousy.

prasangs.title_en: A letter to a grieving friend (Bombay, 1893)
prasangs.summary: Just before sailing for America, he writes to a friend struck by a terrible family loss. Quoting Job, Jesus and the Gita, he says that under the waves there is a depth of calm. He also admits the heart's agony fights against resignation, and prays for strength.
prasangs.lesson: Under the storm of grief there is a deeper calm; it is all right that the heart resists.
prasangs.notes: Interfaith in its sources: the Book of Job, the Beatitudes and Krishna to Arjuna in one short letter.

prasangs.title_en: 'I am drifting': a letter from Alameda (1900)
prasangs.summary: Two years before his death, worn out, he writes that he has laid down the role of leader. He is glad he was born, glad he suffered, glad he made big blunders. He admits that ambition, personality, fear and love of power lay behind his work, and says they are fading as he drifts toward peace.
prasangs.lesson: Honest looking back, with gratitude for the mistakes, can bring peace.

prasangs.title_en: 'Hold on yet a while, brave heart' (poem to the Maharaja of Khetri)
prasangs.summary: A short poem of encouragement to a friend. Clouds hide the sun for a while, summer always follows winter, and no honest struggle is wasted even when hopes fail.
prasangs.lesson: No struggle is wasted; hold on a little longer.

prasangs.title_en: 'Requiescat in pace': for J. J. Goodwin (1898)
prasangs.summary: When his English stenographer and devoted friend Goodwin died young in India, he wrote this farewell. It sends the soul on with blessing and says sweet remembrance fills the place left behind.
prasangs.lesson: Love can bless the one who has gone and let memory fill the gap.
prasangs.notes: Goodwin took down most of the lectures in CW 1–2 in shorthand.

prasangs.title_en: Concentration and detachment
prasangs.summary: All success depends on concentration, but along with it we must build the power to detach, since most suffering comes from a mind stuck on something it cannot let go. If he were educated again, he would train concentration and detachment rather than collect facts.
prasangs.lesson: Train the mind to focus and to let go; both matter.
prasangs.notes: Class notes (CW 6).

prasangs.title_en: Inspired Talks at Thousand Island Park (June 1895)
characters: A small group of American disciples
prasangs.summary: In a summer retreat on an island in the St. Lawrence River, he taught a dozen students daily; Sarah Ellen Waldo took notes. Short sayings: thoughts live and travel far, so guard them; neither seek nor avoid, take what comes.
prasangs.lesson: Guard your thoughts; take what comes without clutching.
prasangs.notes: Disciple's notes, not his own text; wording is as recorded.

prasangs.title_en: Vibhishan crosses over: Ram's refuge speech
prasangs.title_hi: विभीषण का भगवान्‌ श्री रामजी की शरण के लिए प्रस्थान और शरण प्राप्ति
prasangs.summary: Kicked out of Lanka for telling his brother the truth, Vibhishan crosses the sea to Ram, dreaming of his feet. Sugriva wants him bound as a spy; Ram says his vow is to remove the fear of anyone who comes for refuge, and if the visitor were truly wicked he would not have come at all. Ram embraces him, asks how he kept his goodness among the cruel, describes the devotee who ties every thread of love to him, and crowns him king, shyly giving what Ravana got for ten heads.
prasangs.lesson: The turning itself is enough to be taken in; your past is not the deciding question.
prasangs.story_hook: Kicked out by his own brother, a man stood on the far shore and wondered whether the enemy he was walking toward would let him in.
prasangs.notes: Gita Press Sundar 5.42-5.49 (data 5.40-5.47). Overlaps library prasang rcm.p.vibhishan_refuge (rcm.5.40.chaupai.3 to rcm.5.48.chaupai.1), retold here for refuge rather than ethics. rcm.5.42.chaupai.1 and 5.42.chaupai.4 are comfort candidates, listed in ram_existing.jsonl. Leave out 5.41.doha.1 and 5.48.chaupai.1 (harsh lines on those who abandon refugees / worship others).

prasangs.title_en: Valmiki: Ram's vow of refuge and the dove
prasangs.summary: Vibhishana arrives in the sky over Ram's camp. Sugriva argues he should be killed as a spy; Hanuman and Ram disagree. Ram tells the story of a dove that sheltered the hunter who had caught its mate, cites the sage Kandu on protecting whoever asks for shelter, and makes his vow: whoever comes once and says 'I am yours' gets safety from all beings, even if it were Ravana himself.
prasangs.lesson: Refuge is a vow, not a reward for the deserving: once someone says 'I'm yours', they are safe.
prasangs.story_hook: The monkey king wanted the stranger killed; Ram answered with a story about a dove.
prasangs.notes: vr.6.18.31 and 6.18.3 are library cards. Overlaps library prasang vr.p.refuge.

prasangs.title_en: Kevat washes Ram's feet
prasangs.title_hi: केवट का प्रेम और गंगा पार जाना
prasangs.summary: At the Ganga the boatman refuses to row Ram across unless he can first wash his feet, joking that their dust turned a stone into a woman and might turn his boat into one too. Ram, whose name carries the world across, smiles and pleads with him. Afterwards the boatman refuses Sita's ring: today, he says, he has been paid in full.
prasangs.lesson: Love can be playful and stubborn; God enjoys being loved that way.
prasangs.story_hook: The boatman folded his arms and told the prince of Ayodhya he was not getting into his boat until he let him wash his feet.
prasangs.notes: Library prasang rcm.p.kevat covers the same passage; rcm.2.99.chaupai.3 is a library card.

prasangs.title_en: Shabari's wait and the nine forms of devotion
prasangs.title_hi: शबरी पर कृपा, नवधा भक्ति उपदेश
prasangs.summary: An old woman of the forest has waited years for Ram on her teacher's word. When he comes she falls at his feet, washes them, and feeds him fruit he praises again and again. She says she does not know how to praise him; he answers that he recognises only the kinship of devotion, teaches her the nine forms of devotion, and tells her that whoever has even one of them is most dear to him.
prasangs.lesson: Your simple offering is enough; love, not status, is the only kinship that counts.
prasangs.story_hook: For years an old woman swept the path and gathered fruit for a guest she had been told would come.
prasangs.notes: Stop the retelling at Ram's words (3.32.chaupai.4). The episode ends with Shabari entering the fire of yoga (3.32.chhand.1); per product safety, leave that out of cards and retellings. Skip 3.31.chaupai.2-3 and 3.32.doha.1 (caste and gender wording). Valmiki's version (3.74) is library prasang vr.p.shabari; Gitavali 3.17 and the excerpt in tulsi_gv.3.14#2 add her waiting.

prasangs.title_en: Jatayu dies in Ram's lap
prasangs.summary: Searching for Sita, Ram finds the old vulture who fought Ravana to save her, dying. Ram touches his head and the bird's pain leaves. Jatayu refuses Ram's offer to heal him: the one whose name people pray to say at death is in front of his eyes. He asks only for devotion, and Ram, in tears, performs his last rites with his own hands.
prasangs.lesson: Nothing you do for love is small; it is honoured like family.
prasangs.story_hook: An old bird lay broken on the forest floor, holding on to life just long enough to tell Ram what he had seen.
prasangs.notes: Jatayu declining healing (3.27.chaupai.3-4) is acceptance of a natural death, not self-harm, but keep it in the retelling only. Valmiki 3.68 (vr.p.bhakti.jatayu) gives Ram's grief in more detail.

prasangs.title_en: Valmiki: Ram cremates Jatayu like his father
prasangs.summary: Jatayu dies telling Ram where Ravana went. Ram says this loss weighs on him more than Sita's abduction, that the bird is as worthy of honour as his father Dasharatha, builds the pyre himself and performs the rites as for his own kin.
prasangs.lesson: Grief for a loyal friend, even a bird, is real grief; honour it fully.
prasangs.story_hook: Ram had just lost his wife, and yet what broke him that afternoon was the death of an old bird.
prasangs.notes: Library prasang vr.p.jatayu spans 3.50-3.68 (the fight).

prasangs.title_en: Hanuman meets Ram
prasangs.title_hi: श्री रामजी से हनुमानजी का मिलना
prasangs.summary: Sent by a frightened Sugriva, Hanuman goes disguised as a brahmin to question two strangers. When Ram names himself, Hanuman recognises his Lord, falls at his feet speechless, then gently complains that Ram forgot him. He says he knows no method of worship and relies on Ram as a child relies on its mother. Ram lifts him up, holds him, cools him with his own tears, and tells him he is twice as dear as Lakshman.
prasangs.lesson: You don't need the right method; being his is enough, and he weeps to have you back.
prasangs.story_hook: On a mountain path, a monkey in disguise asked two strangers who they were, and then forgot how to speak.
prasangs.notes: Library prasang rcm.p.friendship_pact (4.2.chaupai.2-4.8.chaupai.6) frames it as friendship; this is the devotional frame. rcm.4.4.chaupai.4 is a comfort candidate.

prasangs.title_en: Sugriva: frightened, lifted, forgetful, forgiven
prasangs.title_hi: सुग्रीव का दुःख, बालि वध, सुग्रीव की भूल
prasangs.summary: Sugriva, exiled and robbed by his brother, lives in fear even where Bali cannot reach him. Ram hears him and takes his side; after a first beating, Ram's touch takes the pain away, and Sugriva is made king. Then comfort makes him forget his promise to search for Sita. When he apologises, Ram smiles, says he is as dear as Bharat, and sends him back to work.
prasangs.lesson: Fear is heard, failure is forgiven, and then you get back to the work.
prasangs.story_hook: Even on the safest mountain in the kingdom, Sugriva jumped at every shadow.
prasangs.notes: Bali's killing is morally complex (Ram shoots from hiding); retell it with Ram's own answer and Bali's last words, not as a model. Library prasangs rcm.p.friendship_pact, rcm.p.sugriva_bali and rcm.p.sugriva_forgets cover parts.

prasangs.title_en: Bharat's love: the boon, the meeting, the sandals
prasangs.summary: Bharat, blamed for his mother's plot, asks the holy rivers for nothing but love for Ram, life after life; they tell him he torments himself for nothing. Walking toward Ram, shame slows him and remembering Ram's nature speeds him up. He falls at Ram's feet and Ram lifts him by force into an embrace. He returns with Ram's sandals and for fourteen years runs the kingdom from a hut, asking the sandals' leave for every task.
prasangs.lesson: Love can be lived as responsibility: do the work in the name of the one you love.
prasangs.story_hook: Everyone in Ayodhya assumed Bharat had schemed for the throne; he spent fourteen years proving them wrong from a hut.
prasangs.notes: Spans several library prasangs (rcm.p.bharadwaj, rcm.p.chitrakoot_meeting, rcm.p.ram_bharat_resolution, rcm.p.paduka). Skip 2.176.doha.1 and 2.224.doha.1 (Bharat blames his mother as 'कुमातु').

prasangs.title_en: Sutikshna runs to meet Ram
prasangs.summary: A young sage hears Ram is near and runs out, sure he has no devotion, wisdom or discipline worth anything, trusting only that Ram loves those with nowhere else to go. Lost in love he wanders, dances, forgets the way; Ram watches from behind a tree, then lifts him up and holds him. Asked for a boon, the sage says only: may this one pride never leave me, that I am his.
prasangs.lesson: You don't have to feel qualified; the one with nowhere else to go is the one he loves.
prasangs.story_hook: A young sage ran out of his hut to meet Ram and, halfway there, forgot which way he was going.

prasangs.title_en: Hanuman finds a devotee in Lanka
prasangs.summary: Searching Lanka by night, Hanuman wonders how a good person could live there, then hears someone wake saying 'Ram, Ram'. Vibhishan fears he has no practice or love worth Ram's notice; Hanuman, joking that no one wants to hear a monkey's name before breakfast, says that Ram showed kindness even to him, and weeps remembering it. The two talk of Ram late into the night and find a rest beyond words.
prasangs.lesson: In a hostile place, one friend who shares your faith can be enough.
prasangs.story_hook: In the middle of the enemy's city, at night, a monkey heard someone wake up and whisper the name of his Lord.
prasangs.notes: Library prasang rcm.p.vibhishan_hanuman covers it; rcm.5.6.chaupai.1 is a library card.

prasangs.title_en: Ram cannot repay Hanuman
prasangs.title_hi: हनुमान्‌जी का लौटना, श्री राम-हनुमान्‌ संवाद
prasangs.summary: Back from Lanka, Hanuman tells Ram how Sita survives: his name guards her day and night. Ram, in tears, asks whether one who relies on him can meet calamity; Hanuman answers that the only calamity is forgetting him. Ram says he can never repay Hanuman and cannot even look him in the face; Hanuman falls at his feet and will not get up. Offered anything, he asks only for unwavering devotion, and credits every deed to Ram.
prasangs.lesson: Do the work, give away the credit, and ask only to keep loving.
prasangs.story_hook: Hanuman had burned a city and found the queen; now he lay on the ground in front of Ram and refused to stand up.
prasangs.notes: rcm.5.31.chaupai.5 is a library card.

prasangs.title_en: Valmiki: Hanuman's boon and Ram's debt
prasangs.summary: After the coronation Ram sends his friends home, asking only to be remembered with love. Hanuman asks to live as long as Ram's story is told, so that hearing it can ease his longing. Ram rises from the throne, embraces him, grants it, and says he would give his life for each of Hanuman's services, and hopes Hanuman never falls into trouble that would let him repay it.
prasangs.lesson: The deepest gratitude hopes the other never needs your help.
prasangs.story_hook: When the war was over and the guests were leaving, Hanuman asked Ram for the strangest gift: to keep hearing the story.
prasangs.notes: Source of the belief that Hanuman is present wherever Ram-katha is sung.

prasangs.title_en: Jayant the crow: shelter for the offender
prasangs.summary: Indra's son, disguised as a crow, pecks Sita's foot to test Ram's power. Ram's straw arrow chases him through every world; no god will shelter him. Narada sends him back to Ram, where he falls at his feet admitting he reaped what he sowed. Ram lets him go with the loss of one eye.
prasangs.lesson: Consequences may remain, but the one who turns back is still taken in.
prasangs.story_hook: The crow flew to heaven, to Shiva, to Brahma, and every door closed, until a sage told him to go back to the one he had wronged.
prasangs.notes: 3.2.chaupai.3-4 ('who can save one hostile to Ram') are threats; leave out of cards.

prasangs.title_en: Ram takes the spear meant for Vibhishan
prasangs.title_hi: रामजी का शक्ति को अपने ऊपर लेना
prasangs.summary: In the final battle Ravana hurls a deadly spear at his brother Vibhishan. Remembering his vow to break the pain of those who come to him, Ram pushes Vibhishan behind him and takes the spear on himself.
prasangs.lesson: A promise of shelter is kept with one's own body.
prasangs.story_hook: The spear was aimed at the deserter; Ram stepped in front of it.
prasangs.notes: Kavitavali 6.53 and Gitavali 6.7 add Ram's worry for Vibhishan when Lakshman falls.

prasangs.title_en: The friends who couldn't leave
prasangs.title_hi: पुष्पक विमान पर चढ़कर अवध के लिए प्रस्थान
prasangs.summary: Vibhishan showers jewels from the flying chariot; the monkeys put them in their mouths and spit them out, and Ram, whom sages cannot reach in meditation, laughs with them. He thanks them, tells them to go home and remember him without fear. They stand weeping, unable to speak or leave, so he changes his plan and takes them all to Ayodhya.
prasangs.lesson: Pure love moves God more than any practice; it can even change his plans.
prasangs.story_hook: The war was won and the farewells said, but nobody moved.
prasangs.notes: rcm.6.112.chaupai.3 is a comfort candidate. Library prasang rcm.p.homecoming_haste is adjacent.

prasangs.title_en: The child Ram and the crow
prasangs.summary: The crow-sage Kakbhushundi, after being humbled by the child Ram's play, receives his boon. Ram tells him devotees are always dear to him, that status counts for nothing without love, and gives the parable of a father with many gifted sons whose dearest son is the one who simply loves him, though skilled at nothing. Then the Lord goes back to being a hungry baby and cries until his mother runs to him.
prasangs.lesson: You are loved for loving, not for being impressive.
prasangs.story_hook: The Lord of all the worlds finished his great teaching to the crow, then scrunched up his face and started crying for his mother.
prasangs.notes: Skip 7.85.chaupai.3 (ranking by birth). Library prasang rcm.p.kakbhushundi_pride covers the earlier part.

prasangs.title_en: Tulsidas's petition is signed
prasangs.summary: Tulsidas wrote the Vinay Patrika as a petition to Ram's court. In the last two padas he asks Hanuman, Bharat and Lakshman to mention him at the right moment. Lakshman, reading Hanuman's mind and Bharat's wish, speaks up: one servant has kept faith in the name even in this age. The court agrees, Ram smiles, says he has already taken note, and signs.
prasangs.lesson: After all the pleading, the book ends held: you were already noticed.
prasangs.story_hook: For 277 poems Tulsidas begged to be noticed; in the 279th, Ram picked up the pen.
prasangs.notes: Corpus has the Gita Press bhavartha with the 'रघुनाथ हाथ प्रसंग' (court scene) after pada 279; paraphrased, not copied.

prasangs.title_en: Tulsidas, the boy who begged for scraps
prasangs.summary: Across his later works Tulsidas tells his own story: left by his parents at birth, he wandered door to door for scraps, no job, no trade, no skill, ignored by everyone. Good people told him not to worry; Hanuman raised him like a child; Ram's name, he says, turned a thorny babul into a mango tree. Even when he went astray, he was taken back.
prasangs.lesson: Where you start is not where you end; you can be taken in from nothing.
prasangs.story_hook: The poet of the Ramcharitmanas began life as an unwanted child begging for scraps in the lanes.
prasangs.notes: Spans several works (start/end are the first and last units used, not a contiguous range). Related comfort candidates: tulsi_kv.7.57, tulsi_kv.7.73, tulsi_hb.41, tulsi_dv.109.

prasangs.title_en: Shiva answers Parvati's doubt
prasangs.summary: Parvati, who in a past life as Sati doubted that a grieving prince could be God, now asks Shiva humbly: how can the formless one take a body? Shiva praises her question, bows to the child Ram, and answers that the formless becomes embodied out of love for devotees, and comes whenever good people suffer.
prasangs.lesson: Honest doubt, asked humbly, is welcomed; the answer is love.
prasangs.story_hook: Parvati had once lost everything by doubting quietly; this time she asked out loud.
prasangs.notes: Frame of the whole Manas. Skip 1.107.chaupai.1-4 and 1.108.doha.1-1.109.chaupai.4 (harsh words for non-devotees). Library prasang rcm.p.sati_doubt is the prequel.

prasangs.title_en: Ahalya: the long wait ends
prasangs.summary: On the way to Janakpur, Vishvamitra shows Ram a stone in an empty hermitage: Gautam's wife Ahalya, bearing a curse in a body of stone, longing for the dust of his feet. At his touch she rises, stands before him with folded hands, unable to speak for love, tears streaming, and asks only that her mind may always drink at his feet.
prasangs.lesson: However long you have been frozen, being seen can bring you back to life.
prasangs.story_hook: For years a stone lay in an abandoned hermitage, and only a sage knew it was a woman waiting.
prasangs.notes: Framed fairly: retell without blame and without the curse's backstory. Do not card 1.199.chhand.2 ('मैं नारि अपावन', I am an impure woman) or 1.199.chhand.3 (calling the curse a blessing). No standalone card from this episode.

prasangs.title_en: Draupadi's call and the single leaf of greens
prasangs.title_hi: दुर्वासा का आतिथ्य: द्रौपदी की पुकार और शाक-पत्र
prasangs.summary: Duryodhana sends the short-tempered sage Durvasa and ten thousand disciples to the exiled Pandavas after Draupadi has eaten and the sun-given pot is empty. With no way to feed them, Draupadi calls Krishna in her mind. He arrives at once, asks to be fed first, eats one leaf of greens stuck to the pot, and the sages, bathing in the river, suddenly feel full and flee.
prasangs.lesson: When you have nothing left to offer, calling out is enough; help can come from a single leaf.
prasangs.story_hook: The pot was scraped clean, and ten thousand hungry sages were bathing in the river, expecting dinner.
prasangs.notes: Vulgate/southern episode (Ganguli Vana Parva CCLXI–CCLXII 'Draupadi-harana'; absent from the Critical Edition). Set-up at 3.263 (Duryodhana's plot). 3.264.31 mentions Ambarisha. Avoid the sages' fear of being 'burned' as the moral; the story's heart is Draupadi's call and Krishna's playful arrival.

prasangs.title_en: Draupadi tells Krishna her sorrow
prasangs.title_hi: काम्यकवन में द्रौपदी का कृष्ण से दुःख-निवेदन
prasangs.summary: Krishna visits the exiled Pandavas in the Kamyaka forest and tells Arjuna 'you are mine and I am yours'. Draupadi then comes to him 'seeking refuge with the refuge', tells him, out of closeness, everything done to her in the dice-hall and since, and weeps that she has no one, not even him. Krishna promises she will see justice.
prasangs.lesson: You can bring God your rawest pain, even your sense of being abandoned, and be heard.
prasangs.story_hook: She came to him with her hair still unbound, thirteen years of humiliation in her voice.
prasangs.notes: Krishna's reply (3.12.131–134) is a vow that the Kauravas' wives will weep; the retelling should end on Draupadi being heard and promised justice, not on revenge. 3.12.134 ('the sky could fall… my word won't fail') is a comfort candidate. Udyoga 5.81.20–48 is a parallel scene before the peace mission (anchor 5.81.26, her inner call in the dice-hall); 5.81.36–48 is her demand for war, not card material.

prasangs.title_en: Krishna refuses the king's feast and eats at Vidura's house
prasangs.title_hi: दुर्योधन का भोज त्याग, विदुर के घर भोजन
prasangs.summary: On his peace mission to Hastinapura, Krishna declines Duryodhana's lavish banquet: food is shared out of love or out of need, and here there is neither. He goes instead to Vidura's modest house, eats the simple food offered with devotion, and that night Vidura tells him he cannot describe the joy of seeing him.
prasangs.lesson: God accepts love, not lavishness; a simple meal given with devotion is the real feast.
prasangs.story_hook: The king had laid out gold couches and a banquet; Krishna walked past all of it to a small house down the road.
prasangs.notes: Lies inside the library prasang mbh.p.krishna_peace_embassy (5.71–5.131); this is a sub-episode for story days. The popular detail of Vidura's wife feeding banana peels is from later tradition and Surdas (sur.vp.14), not this text. 5.91.44 (Vidura: 'be pleased with this, our wealth') has a metrically broken pada in data.

prasangs.title_en: Krishna and Bhishma on the bed of arrows
prasangs.summary: After the war, Krishna sits motionless; he explains that the dying Bhishma is thinking of him, so his mind has gone to Bhishma. They visit; Bhishma sings his hymn to Krishna, admits his pain and that he stands only on Krishna's strength. Krishna grants him relief, asks the next morning whether he slept well, and steps back so that Bhishma, not he, will teach Yudhishthira.
prasangs.lesson: The one you think of in your hardest hour is already thinking of you.
prasangs.story_hook: Yudhishthira found Krishna sitting so still that not a hair on his body moved, like a lamp in a windless place.
prasangs.notes: Data 12.45 = Ganguli XLVI, 12.46 = XLVII (Bhishma-stavaraja), 12.51 = LII, 12.53 = LIV. Stavaraja verses 12.46.123–127 are bracketed (other manuscripts); 12.46.123 is phalashruti (one bow = ten horse-sacrifices), excluded. Krishna's boon (12.51.15–16: no pain, hunger or fainting) is grace in the story, never a healing promise on a card.

prasangs.title_en: Bhishma asks Krishna's leave to die
prasangs.title_hi: भीष्म का देहत्याग: श्रीकृष्ण से अनुमति
prasangs.summary: When the sun turns north, Bhishma, after fifty-eight nights on the arrows, takes leave of the family, asks Krishna to protect him and to give him leave to go. Krishna says there is no fault in him and lets him go; Bhishma's last words to the family are to hold to truth and kindness.
prasangs.lesson: At the end, it is enough to say: I am yours; now let me go.
prasangs.story_hook: Fifty-eight nights on a bed of arrows had felt like a hundred years, he said.
prasangs.notes: Data 13.273 = Ganguli Anusasana CLXVII. 13.273.41 'yatah krishnas tato dharmah' recalled here; the card uses the fuller Udyoga form 5.67.9. 13.273.47 ('death stands like your servant') skipped.

prasangs.title_en: Markandeya and the child on the banyan leaf
prasangs.summary: At the end of an age, the sage Markandeya drifts alone over a flooded world and sees a radiant child on a banyan branch. The child draws him inside his body, where he sees all the worlds, then asks if he has been resting, tired. Narayana explains he showed himself because he saw Markandeya's distress. Markandeya tells the Pandavas that this child is Krishna, sitting with them.
prasangs.lesson: When everything you knew is underwater, you have not been forgotten; you are being held.
prasangs.story_hook: The whole world was one dark ocean, and on it floated a single banyan tree with a child asleep on a branch.
prasangs.notes: Data 3.191–3.192 = Ganguli Vana CLXXXVIII–CLXXXIX. 3.192.13 is the Purusha-sukta varna image and 3.192.37 says the sage's pains were 'for his good' (theodicy); neither carded. 3.192.24 has '---' gaps.

prasangs.title_en: The stillborn heir and Krishna's promise
prasangs.summary: Abhimanyu's son is born dead, struck in the womb by Ashvatthama's weapon. Kunti, Subhadra and Uttara beg Krishna for help, reminding him of his promise. Krishna, on the strength of his own truthfulness, revives the child, who is named Parikshit.
prasangs.lesson: In a family's darkest hour, the women's cry is heard and the promise kept.
prasangs.notes: Handle with great care: a child revived from death is not a story for users facing pregnancy or child loss and must never imply that prayer brings the dead back. 14.69.9 (Uttara speaks of poison or fire) is self-harm content, excluded from cards. Use only in a 'refuge stories' context for adults choosing devotion, never in grief plans. 14.66.1 is a placeholder unit ('(94302) / …') in data.

prasangs.title_en: Yudhishthira's question: what is the one refuge?
prasangs.summary: After all the teachings on dharma, Yudhishthira asks Bhishma for the one god, the one refuge, the best dharma. Bhishma answers: praising the imperishable Vishnu with devotion, the purest of the pure and father of beings, and gives the thousand names. In the closing dialogue the Lord says one sincere verse is enough.
prasangs.lesson: After every rule has been explained, the last question is simply: whom do I turn to?
prasangs.notes: Data 13.254 = Ganguli Anusasana CXLIX (southern recension; 274 chapters vs Ganguli's 168). Phalashruti 13.254.125–135 (results by varna, freedom from disease and bondage) excluded. 13.254.147 has small corruptions ('स्या', 'वासुदेव्').

prasangs.title_en: The elephant who finally called (as Surdas sings it)
prasangs.summary: An elephant king is seized by a crocodile in a lake and struggles for a thousand years with all his strength and his herd. Only when his strength is gone does he call out to Hari, who leaves his mount behind and runs barefoot to free him. Surdas returns to the story again and again (vp.11, 21, 241, 256).
prasangs.lesson: Fight with everything you have; when your strength runs out, call. Help comes running.
prasangs.story_hook: For a thousand years the elephant pulled against the crocodile, and for a thousand years his family stood on the bank.
prasangs.notes: The source story is Bhagavata Purana 8.2–4 (not in our data); our anchors are Surdas's retellings. The arc models effort before surrender (cf. Gita 18.63 before 18.66).

prasangs.title_en: Sudama at Krishna's door (as Surdas sings it)
prasangs.summary: Krishna's poor childhood friend Sudama walks to Dwaraka with a handful of rice, ashamed of his poverty. Seeing him from far off, Krishna runs to him and touches his feet, and receives his little gift as if it were everything.
prasangs.lesson: Old friendship and love do not check your bank balance at the door.
prasangs.story_hook: He had only a knotted cloth of rice to bring the king of Dwaraka.
prasangs.notes: Source story Bhagavata 10.80–81 (not in our data); Surdas mentions Sudama in vp.19, 25, 26, 182, 184, 213, 258.

prasangs.title_en: Shvetashvatara: from 'what governs our lives?' to refuge
prasangs.summary: Seekers ask what causes the world and governs their joys and sorrows. Through meditation they come to see one Lord, Rudra-Shiva, hidden in every heart; the Upanishad moves from inquiry to recognition to a prayer of refuge (6.18) and ends on grace and love of God (6.21, 6.23).
prasangs.lesson: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.
prasangs.notes: The arc models surrender after effort and reflection; the Upanishad's God is named Rudra/Shiva but often read as the general Divine.

prasangs.title_en: The gods ask the Goddess: who are you?
prasangs.summary: All the gods come to the Goddess and ask who she is. She answers that she is the highest reality, the source of nature and spirit. The gods bow, praise her as the Mother who protects on every side, and take refuge in her as Durga, who carries beings through hard places.
prasangs.lesson: The Mother who is everything is also near enough to be called on in fear.
prasangs.story_hook: Even the gods did not know who she was, so one day they simply went and asked her.
prasangs.notes: Verses 20-23 (seed-mantra technique) and 31-35 (recitation merit) excluded from cards.

prasangs.title_en: Shiva's grief turns to Ram's name
prasangs.summary: After Sati is gone, Shiva wanders, teaching and singing of Ram, repeating his name. Though beyond desire, he still grieves the loss of his devotee. Seeing his steady love, Ram appears, grateful and kind, praises Shiva's vow and asks him to marry Parvati.
prasangs.lesson: Grief and devotion can walk together; steady love in loss is seen.
prasangs.story_hook: When Sati was gone, the great god of the mountains did not rage or hide; he walked, and he kept saying a name.
prasangs.notes: Sits inside library prasang rcm.p.parvati_tapas (1.61.3-1.80.1); split out as a refuge story. Sati's self-immolation (1.60) not retold on cards.

prasangs.title_en: Rati comes weeping to the god who burned her husband
prasangs.summary: Kama, sent by the gods to break Shiva's meditation, is burned by his third eye. His wife Rati, fainting and weeping, goes straight to Shiva and pleads. Shiva, quick to be pleased and compassionate, promises her that Kama will live on without a body and that she will meet him again when Krishna is born.
prasangs.lesson: Even the one who hurt you can be approached; compassion answers grief.
prasangs.story_hook: The smoke was still rising when the widow walked up to the god who had made it.

prasangs.title_en: Parvati's trust and Shiva's strange wedding
prasangs.summary: The sages tease Parvati that Shiva has burned Kama and her vow is lost; she smiles and trusts him. Shiva arrives with ash, snakes and a wild band of ghosts; Parvati's mother Maina breaks down and blames herself. Parvati comforts her, Narada reveals who Parvati is, and the wedding is celebrated, with Shiva remembering Ram in his heart.
prasangs.lesson: Love sees past appearances; trust can comfort the people who fear for us.
prasangs.story_hook: When the groom arrived, the children of the town ran home screaming.
prasangs.notes: Maina's threat to throw herself and Parvati off a cliff (1.90.chhand.1) and the 'stri-dharma' lines (1.96.chaupai.2-3) are not used on cards.

prasangs.title_en: Parvati asks, and Shiva answers with reassurance
prasangs.summary: On Kailash, Parvati sits beside Shiva and, still carrying her old doubt from her life as Sati, asks how a grieving prince can be God. Shiva is moved to tears, reassures her that there is no doubt left in her heart, and explains that the formless becomes form out of love for devotees. Her confusion lifts 'like autumn heat under moonlight'.
prasangs.lesson: Honest doubt, asked with love, is met with patience, not blame.
prasangs.notes: Harsh lines on scoffers (1.107.chaupai.1-4, 1.108.doha.1-1.109.chaupai.4) left out of cards.

prasangs.title_en: Prahlada, alone after defeat, takes refuge in Narayana
prasangs.summary: With his father killed and his people beaten, the young demon prince Prahlada sees no way out except to take refuge in the very god he feared. He worships Vishnu in mind and in his shrine; the gods doubt a demon can be devoted, but Vishnu tells them he is ready. Vishnu appears, Prahlada sings a hymn of refuge, sinks into realisation and is gently woken to rule with a steady mind.
prasangs.lesson: Refuge is open to anyone, whatever their past; devotion kept up daily changes the mind.
prasangs.story_hook: The palace was full of widows when the boy decided the enemy's god would be his own.
prasangs.notes: Precedes library prasang yv.p.prahlada (5.43, effort and grace).

prasangs.title_en: Shiva teaches Vasishtha what worship really is
prasangs.summary: Shiva and Parvati visit Vasishtha's hermitage; Vasishtha tells Shiva that remembering him has filled his life. Asked how God should be worshipped, Shiva says the true God is awareness itself; its flowers are understanding, evenness and calm, and real worship runs through walking, standing, waking and sleeping, offered with equanimity, compassion and gladness.
prasangs.lesson: Worship can be carried into every hour as calm, kindness and gladness.
prasangs.notes: Merit-reward verses (6a.38.32-36, 'worship for a moment, gain a horse-sacrifice') excluded.

prasangs.title_en: Learned seers find no peace and go to Ganesha
prasangs.summary: Seers who had received all the Vedas still found no peace, so they went to Ganesha's world and took refuge in him. Ganesha tells them that though he has no form, loving devotees see him in the form they long for, and that knowing his highest form brings lasting peace.
prasangs.lesson: Learning alone may not settle the heart; turning to God can.
prasangs.story_hook: They knew every verse of every Veda, and still could not sleep.
prasangs.notes: Heavy OCR noise across the Dheesh Gita.

prasangs.title_en: Overwhelmed sages ask the Sun for a gentle form, and learn devotion
prasangs.summary: The sages ask Surya to show his cosmic form; seeing it, they lose their peace and take refuge, asking for his gentle form again. Surya tells them to fix their minds on him; they admit their minds are restless as wind, and he teaches that devotion is simply the love we feel for friends and family turned toward God.
prasangs.lesson: When the vastness is too much, love is a door small enough to walk through.
prasangs.notes: Closely modelled on Gita 11-12; Hindi-only translation in data; several lines are verbatim Gita verses (skipped).

prasangs.title_en: The ancestors' hymn to Shiva and his easy way
prasangs.summary: Bewildered by Shiva's limitless form, the ancestors praise him and finally hand him the outcome: do whatever is truly good for us. Shiva tells them their work needs a mind joined to him, then gives an easy way: see him everywhere, even in a loving embrace, so devotion never lapses amid hard work.
prasangs.lesson: You can hand over the outcome and still keep working, with devotion woven through.
prasangs.notes: Data mislabels several pitri verses as spoken by Shiva.

prasangs.title_en: The victorious gods praise the Mother's grace
prasangs.summary: After their victory over the demons, the gods praise the Mother, admit their words cannot reach her, and ask forgiveness, adding that even forgiveness comes from her grace. They describe her taking form for devotees' sake and never letting go of those who love her feet.
prasangs.lesson: Grace is not earned by praise; even the clumsy prayer is held.
prasangs.notes: Heavy OCR noise; several verses Hindi-only.

pairs.title: Fate and effort
pairs.idea: Outcomes have five causes; the unseen (daiva) is only one of them. Do your part fully, and when it still goes wrong, don't carry it as your failure.
pairs.rule: Never show rcm.2.165.doha.1 alone. Lead with it for grief and guilt; lead with bg.18.14 for work and failure. Never show rcm.2.165.doha.1 alone. Lead with it for grief and guilt; lead with bg.18.14 for work and failure. Show yv.2.6.1 or yv.2.4.17 only to someone who feels stuck or is making excuses (procrastination, discipline, change_life), never to someone grieving or blaming themselves, and always with yv.2.6.21 in the same plan. For outcome_anxiety and not_promoted, lead with yv.2.7.21 (results come, sooner or later).

pairs.title: No one else gives you sorrow, and it isn't all your fault
pairs.idea: Your peace isn't in others' hands, but that doesn't mean every bad outcome is your doing.
pairs.rule: Pair whenever rcm.2.90.chaupai.2 is shown to someone blaming themselves.

pairs.title: Surrender, after reflection
pairs.idea: Krishna asks Arjuna to think it through fully and choose before he says 'surrender to me'.
pairs.rule: Show 18.63 the day before or alongside 18.66.

pairs.title: Humble first, firm after
pairs.idea: Always start with humility. When it is repeatedly taken for weakness, act firmly, and stop the moment you're heard.
pairs.rule: Lead with rcm.5.48.chaupai.4 (ask politely first). Never show the firm verses on day 1 of a plan or without the three days of patience in the setting.

pairs.title: From 'what's the point?' to working with a free mind
pairs.idea: Rama and Bali both hit 'what is all this for?'. The Yoga Vasishtha's answer is not quitting life but living it fully with an inner anchor, like King Janaka.
pairs.rule: Never show yv.1.12.15, yv.5.22.34, yv.1.10.19 or yv.1.12.22 alone. Follow each, the same day or the next, with yv.6a.115.43 or yv.1.30.17. Use yv.6a.93.29 when the user is considering quitting or running away.

pairs.title: The four gatekeepers: calm, inquiry, contentment, good company
pairs.idea: Four qualities guard the door to a free mind. Start with any one; each strengthens the others.
pairs.rule: Use as a 4-day mini-plan: day 1 up_maha.150 (the list) or yv.2.16.19; then one gatekeeper per day (calm 2.13.64, inquiry 2.14.11, contentment 2.15.11, good company 2.16.8); close with yv.2.16.32 (one virtue grows the others).

pairs.title: Effort and grace
pairs.idea: The Yoga Vasishtha's strong case for effort does not reject devotion: sometimes we wake by our own effort, sometimes by grace reached through devotion, and daily practice ripens the mind.
pairs.rule: For users in doubt_faith or reconnect_faith, show yv.5.43.9 before or with any paurusha card, so effort doesn't read as anti-devotional.
